speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
On page 25 of yesterday's La Presse, under an eye-catching headline, it is written:
Caouette said to have ordered all members of his group to hand over to him $3,000 out of their pay.
The article is signed by Marcel Gingras and reads as follows:
The leader of the Ralliement Creditistes, Mr. Real Caouette, is reported to have given 24 hours to the members of his group to hand him over a sum of $3,000 that each had promised to pay him.
And a little further on, one may read:
Each had been so happy about his raise in sessional indemnity that all the Caouette followers accepted the deal. Yesterday was the day of reckoning, but two of them are said to have refused to cough up, and it was then that the leader of the Ralliement is supposed to have issued his ultimatum.
Mr. Speaker, those are false insinuations and rumours bordering on stupidity. I do hope that the correspondent, Mr. Gingras, will show some professional integrity and give my denial as much space as he gave to those foolish statements which are quite typical of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer).
Mr. Speaker, since, unfortunately, I have to leave Ottawa today to keep an engagement in my riding tomorrow morning, with your permission and the unanimous consent of the house, I wish to take this opportunity to say how happy I am to be able to thank you for the courtesy and fairness you have shown us during the session that is drawing to a close.
May I offer you also my best wishes for Christmas, as well as to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), to the cabinet members, to the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), to all the leaders of the other parties as well as to all the members of the house and to the staff.
I am looking forward to seeing you again in 1964.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice was going to make a statement today on the Wasylen-chuk case. I wonder whether he is prepared to do so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am. I do so in answer to a question raised by the Leader of the Opposition and also one raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but it has to do chiefly with a question put by the Leader of the Opposition with regard to whether or not my parliamentary secretary had any communications with others in connection with this matter.
The statement is as follows. After the extradition warrant had been sent out a telephone call was received by my parliamentary secretary from Mr. Ray Perrault, speaking for himself and on behalf of what he described as a legal committee, asking for further consideration of the point that Wasy-lenchuk ought not to be surrendered for extradition because he was on parole, and for consideration of the point that the habeas corpus judge had not actually issued an order dismissing the application.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Mr. Perrault indicated that the execution of the warrant was imminent and suggested to Mr. Macdonald that he should telephone the warden of Oakalla prison with a view to delaying execution of the warrant while these points were being considered. Mr. Macdonald complied with the request, and when he reached the warden he was informed that Wasylenchuk was already in the custody of United States officers and on his way to the United States.
With reference to the question raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam with regard to my looking into the point having to do with section 24 of the Extradition Act and section 11 of the Parole Act, I have this to say. I do not wish to be drawn into a legal argument, and I do not believe it would be in accordance with the practice for me to engage in one. Therefore I shall restrict myself simply to saying that I have been advised by the legal officers of my department that neither by force of section 24 of the Extradition Act nor section 11 of the Parole Act, nor both, is a person who is at large on parole to be considered as a person who is, to use their words, "undergoing sentence" within the meaning of the Extradition Act.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. In view of the confusion surrounding the extradition I wonder if the minister would not see fit to table the so-called opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not a socalled opinion. It is an opinion, a verbal opinion that was given to me by the officers when the matter was under discussion prior to the statement I made the other day and again today.

As I said the other day, I must be guided, as every minister of justice must be guided, by the advice I receive from the officers and not by advice received from members of parliament. That is what I was guided by when I made the statement yesterday and when I, in effect, repeated it today.

Inquiries of the Ministry

It was after that that the point was considered; in fact two points were raised, and I might as well give them to the house.
The first point was that the proceedings had not been properly signed by the judge in question. This was gone into, and it was seen immediately that was not the case. The next question was whether a person who is on parole is subject to extradition. The opinion was given by our officers, and they have communicated it to me on several occasions, that according to their interpretation of these two sections a person who is on parole under these circumstances can be extradited.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REFUSAL TO COMMUTE SENTENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with reference to the Coffin case I promised that before the house rose I would make a short statement and I have it here. On Tuesday of this week I said I was studying, in co-operation with the officers of the department, what happened prior to the refusal to commute the sentence of Coffin and that I hoped to be able to make a statement in that regard before the adjournment of the house.
Since making that statement I have spent a very considerable amount of time reviewing the file with the officers of the department, and to avoid any misunderstanding I should say that what I have seen so far indicates that representations regarding the significant matters raised in the book, except the incident of the Indian, Thompson, were before the department and considered by it before the decision was taken not to commute the sentence. Nothing I have seen so far has pointed to the desirability of any different kind of inquiry from what I have been making.
The incident concerning the Indian, Thompson, arose, of course, subsequent to the carrying out of the sentence. Nevertheless I cannot say that in the time at my disposal I have been able to go into the matter sufficiently, at first hand, to state a final conclusion. I shall therefore have to defer my definitive statement to a later date. I would hope to have it ready in the not too distant future. I am sorry for this delay, but as I indicated on a previous occasion I believe that the seriousness of the issue requires care rather than haste.

Mr. Speaker, before we proceed with the study of the bill and while we are still at the resolution stage, it seems to me it would be appropriate for the Minister of Public Works to make a statement concerning some problems which are being raised in relation with this measure to amend the world exhibition legislation.
I should like to put a few questions to the Minister of Public Works, and I hope he will be able to answer them so as to enlighten the people on the many problems that have come up in these last four months, or more, with regard to the world fair.
First, I should like to ask the Minister of Public Works what are the reasons which prompted him to defer the official decision pertaining to the choice of the present site.
I also asked sometime ago whether the minister was aware of the technical problems involved in the filling of Notre Dame island. It seems to me that it would be in order for him to tell us how it is that instead of removing daily about 20,000 cubic yards of filling material from the bed of the river, only 3,000

cubic yards are taken out, which does not seem to be consistent with the reports given to us these last weeks about the possibility of handing the land over to the corporation by June 1964, as provided by the act.
I should also like to ask the minister whether the bill is now before us merely in order to increase the salary of the members of that crown corporation, or if the amendment is intended to extend its administrative framework?
I think that it would be in order also for the Minister of Public Works to assure us that this amendment to the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation Act is not another excuse to open the door to patronage, for it has been noticed for some time that several appointments have been made in favour of persons who are very close to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) and, moreover, those persons have been seen with him during the official proceedings to receive the new commissioner general.
Moreover, I should like to get an answer from the minister to the following question. We have been trying for four months already to know what salaries will be paid to the commissioner general and to his deputy.
Mr. Chairman, those are all questions that must be answered.
I wonder what prevented the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) from telling us until now what will be the salary of the commissioner general.
The minister has assured us on several occasions that we were going to receive this information within a few days. This question goes back to July of this year. Nearly five months have elapsed since, and we have not received the expected answers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. Mary has raised five questions which I will try to answer as briefly as possible, while trying at the same time to give him satisfaction.
As far as the allegations that there has been a delay in the selection of the site are concerned, I must state that there has been no delay. The former prime minister, in a wire which he sent in March 1963, admitted in principle the selection of the present site.
Likewise, we have confirmed the same choice in May. We said that we reserved the right to acknowledge formally the selection of this site as soon as the engineers' report would have assured us of the feasibility of holding the exhibition on that site. In July, we received a report from the Lasalle laboratories and, two or three days later, we came to an agreement with the province and the city of Montreal.

I must point out to the hon. member for St. Mary that the municipal engineers of Montreal, who are paid by the city, imposed two conditions concerning the present site, that is the building of a breakwater upstream from the Champlain bridge and of a sill downstream.
Consequently, we discussed the matter with the engineers and, as I said a moment ago, we signed an agreement only two or three days after we received the report. So there was no delay in making the decision.
As for the difficulties which the city of Montreal is encountering in connection with the filling operations which are being carried out on St. Helen's and Notre Dame islands, I must say to my hon. friend that I am aware of that fact just as well as he is or anybody else because there has been mention of it in the press. However, this matter is covered by a tripartite agreement among the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal and the federal government. Under the agreement, the city is to deliver the present site by June 1964. It was to be expected that there would be difficulties.
The hon. member must know that, only two days ago, the mayor of Montreal again confirmed that the site would be ready on time. Let us leave it to the Montreal authorities to provide the site and to respect the commitments made.
With regard to the bill now before us, it does not provide for any fundamental amendments, though it involves amendments of some importance. The purpose of this bill is to amend the title of the act and the reference to the site of the exhibition, so as to specify that it will not necessarily be located on the island of Montreal. Third, it provides for the establishment of an executive committee, for an increase from 12 to 14 in the number of directors, and for the allowances payable to the directors, the commissioner general and the deputy commissioner general.
There is also a clause dealing with the retirement of employees. Another clause is meant to protect the symbols referring to the exhibition, which must remain its property in order that they may not be used for general business purposes. When my hon. friend referred to the increase of directors from 12 to 14 he said a word about the possibility of patronage. I can reassure him because when I met the former commissioner general, Mr. Paul Bienvenu, as well as his successor, Mr. Dupuy, I clearly explained to them that we expected that the heads of the exhibition would organize an exhibition worthy of Canada and that we were leaving them the entire responsibility of the administration.

I can say that all appointments were made by the directors of the fair and we did not make any suggestions. The only intervention by the government is about the appointments to be made only by the governor in council.
With regard to the salary of the commissioner general, there is nothing unusual about that. If I was unable to give the hon. member an answer until now, the same holds true today. The commissioner general of the fair is still on the establishment of the external affairs department, he is still our ambassador to Paris, but I can tell my hon. friend that the matter will be settled in January.
On the other hand, I can give an answer immediately to the hon. members about the salary of the deputy commissioner; I speak from memory and if my reply is not accurate, I will correct myself in a while after consulting my officials.
The deputy commissioner general will receive a salary of $35,000 a year.
I think that takes care of the questions of the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I have a supplementary question to ask the Minister of Public Works.

I would also have liked the minister to deal a little longer with the reasons which led to the resignation of Messrs. Paul Bienvenu and Carsley. I come back on that point because the minister is aware of the fact that Mr. Paul Bienvenu had sent his resignation to the Prime Minister of Canada during the month of July and when I asked a question on July 18, asking whether it was true that Mr. Bienvenu was about to resign, the Prime Minister replied that there was nothing true in those allegations and that everything was fine and dandy; yet, he had in his hands a letter dated

World Exhibition Corporation Act July 8 to the effect that Mr. Paul Bienvenu had informed him of his intention to resign.
Therefore, the Prime Minister's answer was inconsistent with the facts, and I think the Minister of Public Works has the responsibility to set things straight.
I take this opportunity to congratulate Messrs. Paul Bienvenu and Carsley for their tremendous and admirable effort while they were in office. Besides, statements of appreciation were published in every newspaper.
I should like to point out to the house that Messrs. Paul Bienvenu and Carsley accepted to work without pay or indemnity while the deputy commissioner will receive a $35,000 salary, and we do not yet know what the chief commissioner's salary will be.
I think it is quite illogical for a crown corporation to hire someone without even knowing if a salary will be paid to him and to make him work without knowing whether he will be paid or not.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that both the house and the public should know the amount of that salary and the terms of employment.
I am of course very happy about the appointment of Mr. Dupuy and of his deputy, for they are both very able men; however, I would like to get more precise explanations as to the reasons which prompted Messrs. Bienvenu and Carsley to resign; I am also curious to learn why the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Public Works have given us such evasive, and even inaccurate answers?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) has asked five questions, which I am quite happy to answer.
As to the appointment of Mr. de Belle-feuille, I understand that he will have nothing to do with public relations. I believe his official title is something like "director of the exhibitors". As for his appointment, I must say that before it was made, I got a letter from the world exhibition authorities, recommending that Mr. de Bellefeuille be given the position of director of the exhibitors.
Having looked into the bylaws, we pointed out to the fair directors that they were under no obligation to consult the government as to that appointment, which fell under their jurisdiction, and that the governor in council appoints only the commissioner general and his deputy.
It was after that exchange that Mr. de Bellefeuille was appointed, and the federal government had nothing to do with that appointment. I am happy to say that we are delighted with Mr. de Bellefeuille's appointment; he is a very able man, and we feel that he will do an excellent job.

Concerning the appointment of two additional directors, I think this is very important. It was pointed out that under the former organization, various regions of the country were not represented, so as to give that organization a national character. Now, as this will not be a Montreal or a Quebec exhibition but indeed an exhibition which must be an accomplishment of the whole of Canada, the government thought it appropriate to appoint two more directors, in order to give the organization a more adequate national representation.
As to the actual reasons for the resignations of Messrs. Bienvenu and Carsley, I must tell the house that I have nothing to add to the letters of resignation which were handed in to the Prime Minister some months ago. Furthermore, I believe Messrs. Bienvenu and Carsley gave information to the press in addition to that contained in their letters.
I agree with my hon. friend that these were resignations that caused much regret in all circles, and I should also state that I wrote a personal letter to Messrs. Bienvenu and Carsley, with whom I was well acquainted, not only to express my regrets but also to tell them how much the government appreciated the work they had accomplished since the laborious beginnings of the exhibition.
Mr. Chairman, I do not speak this way because the previous government was implied or because the former prime minister was responsible for the establishment of that organization. It is normal that the beginnings of an undertaking such as the world exhibition should be complicated and difficult; but once the organization has taken shape, so to speak, the task becomes much easier.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for St. Mary stated that the former commissioner general and his deputy had offered their services free. That statement is true, and I believe that this has not been sufficiently known in the public. I am glad the hon. member has brought this up, so that the public at large will know that Messrs. Bienvenu and Carsley had no other ambition than to help their country by placing their wide experience at the service of the Canadian people free of charge.
But today, the situation is different. The commissioner general and his deputy have to face a tremendously difficult job and we thought it fair, in the circumstances, that both of them be paid. Actually I think that neither the hon. member for St. Mary nor any other member will want to question the fact that a reasonable salary should be paid to people who now have to work from 15 to 17 hours a day.

Mr. Chairman, I think that 1 have dealt with all the questions of the hon. member for St. Mary. If I have overlooked certain points, I am sure that he will raise them again.

Mr. Chairman, I do not
desire to ask any particular questions of the minister, but rather to make some comments and express my view that this resolution and such a bill-because we have now seen the bill and therefore have more knowledge of what is in the government's mind than would ordinarily be the case-should be opposed. I for one want to indicate that I have grave doubts and reservations about proceeding any further along this line that we have been following in the last few months since the passage of the original act.
Because of the progress that the resolution, and the bill which will follow, have had in the house so far, it seems to me there is some reluctance on the part of the government itself about this measure; because in the first instance the bill was introduced improperly, as Mr. Speaker ruled, and surely the extreme knowledge which the members of the cabinet, especially the Secretary of State, have about the rules should have warned them that the bill was going to be out of order on the grounds that is was not preceded by a resolution. Following upon that, the various delays that have taken place in calling this resolution indicate even more strongly to me that the government is not that anxious to participate in the particular project which will take place.
It was originally conceived that this would be a Canadian project, expressive to an extent of the Canadian viewpoint, and to coincide with our one hundredth birthday in 1967. In fact the speeches made in the house on the occasion of the passage of the original act reflected this desire for Canadianism, Canadian participation, and that a national concept be shown in the world fair itself, but unfortunately it has degenerated from something of a national scope to something not only provincial in nature but almost restricted to a city.
Even the Hansard index, which all hon. members have, indicates this; because in the index, if you look under the heading "Canadian World Exhibition Corporation" you will find a subheading which says "Montreal", and under the heading "Montreal" there are listed the references to the world fair. That is where you find all the references, not under "Canadian World Exhibition Corporation" but under "Montreal world fair".
While the goal may initially have been Canadian, I submit primarily that the force
World Exhibition Corporation Act behind this concept is that of Quebec and the pressure is that of Mayor Jean Drapeau of the city of Montreal, who incidentally, I understand, is a gentleman who absolutely detests those of English background and those who speak the English language, and this is regrettable and unfortunate.
I have reservations about supporting this measure because if all the indications we have had in the past are carried out, then this to me is not a national project or something which would reflect the concept of Canadian expression, or full Canadian participation in the fair. Primarily it is to be a sort of monument to the mayor of Montreal himself, and the minister has said that the expansion of the directors from 12 to 14 was designed to deal with this problem and make the fair more national in scope and application. But even though the number of directors is to be increased from 12 to 14, half of them are going to be chosen specifically and directed by the lieutenant governor of the province of Quebec and the other seven are to be chosen by the governor in council, presumably to give a more national application to this particular organization.

However, there are always exceptions, as the hon. member for St. Mary has pointed out, and it is to the exceptions that I intend to direct my attention. In the first place I am going to refer to the bill, if I may, because it has already been spoken of by the minister. He stated a moment ago that the two directors to be appointed would be appointed by the governor in council. But the bill does not say that; the bill says the very reverse. Clause 3 (2) says:
Of the fourteen other directors referred to in subsection (1), seven shall be appointed on the recommendation of the lieutenant governor in council.
World Exhibition Corporation Act
I think a change will have to be made in this regard. An amendment will have to be made so as to bring this section into line with the arrangements which have been made by the minister with the government of Quebec.
We are facing a very difficult problem. I think there has been gross delay on the part of the government in connection with launching the world fair. Canadians as a whole have a great stake in national prestige to assure the success of this project. No one yet knows what the total expenditure will be. There has been an estimate of $585 million as the total cost, an estimate I think made by Mr. Bienvenu some months ago. I feel we should receive very full information on this matter before passing the bill which will be before us following passage of this resolution.
This fair is to be representative of Canada. It is not a sectional fair, and that has been so recognized both by the province of Quebec and by the mayor and council of the city of Montreal. There is no question in my mind about the desire of the government of Quebec and the capacity of that province, with the rest of Canada, to make this fair a monument to confederation, a monument to better understanding between the races. That monument is to mark a new era of progress in national unity. But those objectives will not be attained by the haphazard, zigzag courses which are being taken since this government assumed office.
Mention has been made of the statute; that it provided for this fair to be sited on the island of Montreal. I recall very well discussions taking place in this connection when I was prime minister. I agree quite frankly, on the basis of the representations and views of the government of the province of Quebec and of the corporation of the city of Montreal, that a change in this regard would be desirable. But I pointed out that any action in this respect must result and stem from a statute passed by parliament. I can understand the delays which have taken place to provide for the amendment required to establish as the site of the fair St. Helen's island rather than some other location on the island of Montreal.

Very definitely not.
There were discussions which took place then on the passage of the legislation. In the month of March representations were made that on the basis of full consideration of all the elements, the appropriate place would be St. Helen's island. I made it clear that because of the suggestion made by the secretary general, the assistants and the directors, with the concurrence of the government of the province of Quebec and of the city council of the city of Montreal, legislative amendments would be brought before parliament so as to give parliament the opportunity to make that alteration. But what has happened is this. The present government has been in office since April 22, and parliament has been sitting fairly steadily since May 20. During all this time work has been proceeding which is totally illegal, unlawful and beyond the rights of those carrying it out. I found it passing strange that the Prime Minister of Canada should be attending the opening ceremonies on an island which, as yet, has received no designation from parliament.
I agree as to the necessity of the change, but as to the action so far taken, which has been to proceed without proper authorization, I would point out that the executive has no authority to act contrary to the statute, that parliament is supreme in these matters. We are in favour of the amendment, but I am pointing out that every action taken to date has been legally improper and totally beyond the authority given by parliament.
To say this in no way detracts from the fact that every support will be given by the opposition to changing the location on the basis of the verbal arrangements made and the subsequent confirmation of the site by the present government. Nevertheless, the action taken to date by the government and its representatives has been altogether beyond the rights of those concerned. I know that the Minister of Public Works, who is an excellent lawyer, will be the first to agree that what has been done has been illegal. He affirms that. Parliament is now being asked-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the adjournment I was dealing with the problem created by the delays, and had mentioned the very lengthy delays and the fact that whatever work has been done on this location, ratified as I know it will be by parliament, is none the less illegal and improper. The government should have brought in this legislation immediately the session was under way, and if it had done so what has taken place subsequently would not have occurred.
There are one or two other observations I want to make. We want to get information. Today we received information as to the salary that the associate director is going to receive, but we have had no information as to what the director is going to receive. Naturally we are all very anxious to bring this session to a conclusion, and the easiest way to do that is to furnish information. The government is in a position to furnish that information, and must have available to it knowledge of the amount that will be paid the director general.
In that connection I want to mention Mr. Bienvenu and Mr. Carsley. These men accepted their positions because of their belief that by doing so they could do something worth while on behalf of their country. They

asked no fee; they asked no salary. When asked to serve they simply agreed to do so. We should have the information I have mentioned.
We should also have information as to the total expected expenditure to be made on this fair. I do not want to reiterate what I have already said, but this fair cannot fail. To allow this fair, representative of this nation, even to enter the spectrum of failure would give to Canada a black eye internationally. In that connection I want the minister to let us know how many nations have agreed to participate. Months have gone by. Is it a fact that so far only two nations have agreed to send exhibits?
The next question I ask is this. Is there any foundation for the widely spread rumour that the government has in mind the possibility of postponing the date of the fair from the year of the hundredth anniversary of this nation to a later year? I hope there is no foundation for that. To do so would be to follow a course of defeatism and despair, and would give our country a reputation that would be far from favourable.
I would also point out that a few weeks ago information was sought in the house by the hon. member for St. Mary. He has been asking for information, as has the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. None has been forthcoming. There has always been the suggestion that if you just wait in hope and expectation you will ultimately be given information. Certainly there has been no application of the principle, ask and ye shall receive, when it comes to information in connection with this fair.
I ask this question. Will Mr. Pierre Dupuy give up his position as ambassador? There was a suggestion that this matter might be resolved in the month of January. I have a great regard for Mr. Pierre Dupuy. As a matter of fact I made the recommendation that he be ambassador to France following my experience with him in Rome in 1954 when he was ambassador there. I found there was nothing he would not do to make Canadian visitors to Italy welcome, and would personally do everything possible to make their stay convenient. I found him a very wise counsellor and I was greatly impressed by him. But he cannot do two jobs.
When listening today to the Minister of Justice speaking of when we might get information in regard to a case in British Columbia that received consideration in the house this morning, I saw in his eyes that glow that indicates that an ambassadorship may well be the resting place of the Minister of Justice. If that be so, I would say that Canada would be better represented there by him than it is
World Exhibition Corporation Act in his occupancy of the position of Minister of Justice. I do not know whether that vacancy is going to take place, but I am just trying to find out. I am not seeking information as to identity at the moment, but no one can deny me the speculative right to contemplate the possibilities of a final resting place being found.
I should also like to secure some information that has been asked for and promised over and over again. What are the expected fair costs? I refer to an article that appeared in the press on October 10, in which it was stated that Mr. Shaw, the deputy commissioner general, was bubbling with appreciation of the site and disclosed certain things in an interview. The article points out that Mr. Shaw is a good humoured man and tries to answer all questions put to him. He did not appear to know definitely, but he did say that within a matter of six weeks the costs of the fair and the estimates would be available. The Minister of Public Works himself, having been asked a similar question in the house, also stated that full information would be available by December 20. I would ask the minister to place before the house, first in general and then in particular, the developments that the fair directors have in mind, the cost of each of the several items, and the extent to which any advances towards the building of these fair devices have been attained.
These are some of the matters upon which information has been requested. We have not been able to get anything but generalities, and the time has now come when the house and the country should be assured, finally and absolutely, that this fair is going to be a success; that it is going to achieve the objectives and purposes that the government in which I had the honour to be prime minister had in mind when it made the application on behalf of Canada to secure this fair.
It is well for the record to go back and review, very shortly, something of the course taken. It was in 1958 that the late Senator Mark Drouin suggested, when he was at the Brussels exhibition, that Canada might hold a fair in 1967 to coincide with the centennial celebrations. In 1959 the Montreal chamber of commerce prepared a brief. In 1960, on February 10, I announced that Canada would apply to I.B.E. for the fair; that Ottawa would guarantee $20 million, Quebec $15 million and the city of Montreal $5 million. On March 7, 1960 Canada was informed officially that Russia would apply for the 1967 fair to commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of the communist revolution. We tried very hard to secure the fair at that time. On May 5, 1960 the U.S.S.R. on the fifth ballot received a

World Exhibition Corporation Act majority of the votes in the meeting of the I.B.E. In 1961 the U.S.S.R. decided it would not go ahead.
Once more a movement began for a new application. In June, 1962 Premier Lesage confirmed the provincial promise of $15 million. On September 7 the then government announced it would apply for the fair. On November 13, 1962 the 1967 exhibition was awarded to Canada by the international bureau of expositions. There have been many articles on the subject pointing out the delays that have taken place since April 21. There was an exhaustive article by Mr. Bernard Dufresne of the gallery, which appeared in the Globe and Mail on August 30. It reads as follows:
When things go wrong in French Canada they say, "Ca ne tourne pas rond." A rough translation could be "The wheels are turning off centre," but the best idiomatic equivalent is: "Things are in a mess."
I hope there is no foundation for the fears expressed in that article and that the minister will set out in detail what the plans are, how far progress has been made, and what will be the total amount of expenditure for Canada. What is the consensus as to the buildings that are to be erected? We should like to know, before we leave here, if this legislation is amended as requested, what advances will be made toward the attainment of that objective which must be dear to the hearts of all of us, namely the success of the fair. I have seen a fine spirit of cooperation between the provincial government and the mayor and corporation of the city of Montreal. I hope the same co-operation will be available to the federal government. However, there has been nothing yet to indicate a recognition that time is of the essence and that action must be taken.
As for regularizing what has been done illegally in starting the work on St. Helen's island without amending the act of parliament, that is passed now. I do not like to see legislation after the event. It is the kind of retroactive legislation that has inherent in it dangerous possibilities. However, the work has been done. We intended, when we were in office, to introduce legislation, but the exigencies of elections brought about a change which denied that legislation. This government followed the views we had expressed in the months of February and March and made a decision that the St. Helen's island site would be the one. However, they did not bring legislation before parliament. I ask, what was the reason for the delay? I cannot understand it. There has been legislation brought before us of little or no consequence, while this is of the utmost importance to Canada. Canada will suffer an


international degradation, a national loss of prestige that this parliament and the Canadian people cannot possibly dissipate.
I want to say again that I hope the minister will give us the facts and answer these questions. Let us know how much is going to be paid for holding this fair. Let us know what is going to be expended. What are the plans? He could have gained the co-operation of all members and brought on the activity that has been lacking if he had introduced this amendment rather than sitting back and holding this important legislation to the last minute of the last hour of the last two days of this session.

Mr. Chairman, I think I can count on the house's permission at this time to answer the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and then the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I listened with some dismay to the comments of the hon. member for Skeena.
Surely, the hon. member for Skeena is aware that we shall soon be celebrating Christmas and the new year and wishing for peace on earth and good will to men, and I do not exclude the hon. member from the group of men of good will. However, when he comes back for the next session, if he reads over and meditates on what he said this morning, I do not think he will care to repeat it. I am sure of that and I do not wish to reply in detail to everything he said.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred to co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal governments. He recognized that such co-operation existed and was essential to the success of such a gigantic undertaking as the world exhibition, where the prestige of Canada is at stake.

I would like to refer immediately to a few points raised by the Leader of the Opposition. As far as the allegation of delays is concerned, I wonder whether the Leader of the Opposition is in a position to state clearly what he has in mind. I have followed this undertaking since the month of April, and last May we confirmed approval in principle of the site of the fair. If the Leader of the Opposition had been the head of the government from April to July, I am sure he would not have come to an effective agreement with the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal to begin the work without there having been proper surveys and studies carried out by engineers. In fact, Mr. Chairman, the city of Montreal knew only in July that the site was a feasible one. They did not know this until they received the report of the Laboratoire Lasalle

after innumerable studies had been made, and then the three governments were in a position to examine this report and take proper steps.
I repeat what I said this morning. In the same week that the final report of the Labo-ratoire Lasalle reached my office, an agreement was made with the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec. I again say that I reject any allegation of delays as far as we are concerned.

I was coming to that, Mr. Chairman. I would be ready to admit that technically the right hon. gentleman is right. The reason we are increasing the number of directors from 12 to 14 is that we would like to improve the image of the organization; we would like more regions of this country to be represented. The right hon. gentleman will find in the bill before us that the same number of directors, namely seven, is provided for Quebec and for the federal government, though we are going to appoint two additional directors. The reason is that because the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal will bear half the total expenditures, we thought that at least in the statute they should provide the same number of directors as the federal government. This number is seven. But I wish to state, Mr. Chairman, and I do not hesitate for a moment to commit myself by saying, that the two additional directors will be appointed by the governor in council. A gentlemen's agreement was reached between the federal government and the government of Quebec. I hope hon. members will be satisfied with my statement.
The right hon. gentleman also claimed that we should have presented to the house before now an amendment to the act in order to legalize the description of the site. I wish to state that we were planning to present this
World Exhibition Corporation Act amendment immediately after the house resumed in September, but because we thought we would be making additional amendments it was considered preferable to wait and present all the amendments at the same time. Because the leader of the official opposition may think he has a prima facie case of illegality, may I state first of all that the government of the province of Quebec last summer passed an act in which it is stated very clearly that Notre Dame island belongs to the city of Montreal.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, may I say that the federal government has not yet spent one nickel in relation to the site. I repeat, not one nickel has been spent by the federal government in relation to the site. I repeat also that the site is the sole responsibility of the city of Montreal, and they have the obligation to deliver this site before the end of June, 1964. A budget was prepared for the year 1963, and it has to do with salaries and details of the organization. There was no mention of any other undertaking or construction project.
I now come to the question of salary of the chief commissioner. I repeat that this question has not been settled as yet but will be settled sometime in January. Until then the chief commissioner will continue to enjoy the salary and indemnities as ambassador, which post he is still occupying.

Mr. Chairman, I want to take this opportunity to say a few words and to express to the Minister of Public Works my best wishes for the success of the world exhibition in 1967.
On the other hand, I want to state that I am sorry about the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I think that all members of this house, with the exception of the hon. member for Skeena, feel that His Honour Mayor Drapeau, of Montreal, is anxious to co-operate with everyone, at all levels, so that the world exhibition might be a success.
The mayor of Montreal must be commended for giving of his time, his energy and his talent in order that the city of Montreal may contribute, directly or indirectly, to the success of that exhibition. Actually, the world exhibition is not the responsibility of Mayor Drapeau only, but also of the Quebec government and of the federal government, with, of course, the co-operation of the foreign countries which will have a pavilion at the fair. This is an undertaking on a national scale and not on a municipal scale, as suggested by the hon. member for Skeena.
I would like to ask the minister why we must wait so long to have Mr. Dupuy's status determined? Mr. Dupuy is in charge of the fair, but he is still the Canadian ambassador in Paris. I wonder why he has not yet been asked to devote himself exclusively to the fair since, as the minister said, it is a tremendous venture which certainly requires, to my mind, the undivided attention of Mr. Dupuy.
I have a suggestion for the minister: at the very first opportunity, he should replace Mr. Dupuy by the Minister of Justice, Mr. Chevrier. I think that would provide a speedy settlement of the problem.
As far as developing of the exhibition site is concerned, that is the development of the islands, it seemed to be understood that the filling material would cost some $12 million. I should like to ask the minister whether it is true that it will cost $60 million because the

required material cannot be taken from the bottom of the St. Lawrence river since there are several feet of sheet of rock.
I think the authorities concerned will have to see to it that the filling is well done, because taking the New York world exhibition statistics in 1939-1940, public services involved 10 miles of sewers, 20 miles of drains, 15 miles of water pipes and 16 miles of gas lines. This means that the authorities concerned will have to see to it that the ground is well settled in order to avoid pipe breakage for instance.
Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition quite properly asked what would be the total cost of that gigantic undertaking. I have some information from an authority very close to the world exhibition concerning the approximate costs for the various administrative levels to carry out that project. For instance, the total investment is estimated at $580,540,000, of which $82,300,000 are chargeable to the exhibition corporation, $83,740,000 to the city of Montreal, $141,500,000 to the province, $70,500,000 to the federal government, $104 million to foreign countries and $98.5 million to Canadian private enterprise. So the total investment will come close to $1 billion.
The management anticipates expenditures of over $80 million, without taking into account administrative expenditures which will certainly add up to several millions. To meet that tremendous responsibility, I understand the exhibition corporation only has the $40 million put at its disposal by the three governments. Since the total revenue is estimated as some $40 million, based on the estimates already prepared for the New York exhibition, a large operation deficit is already anticipated.
Then we would appreciate, if the minister without entering into details would at least tell the house, whether it is true that, as I have been told by someone who is very close to world exhibition, the total cost would reach a billion?
The minister has also spoken about the Canadian pavilion. I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works whether it is true, even if this matter comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, that the cost of the Canadian pavilion will reach $21 million. We, on this side of the house, would appreciate receiving this information.
Mr. Chairman, those were the remarks which I wanted to make. However, as for the approximate cost of this venture, I would be pleased if the minister would give us further explanations.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up too much of the time of the house this afternoon.
First of all, as member for a constituency where all races live together in a genuine spirit of national unity, I simply want to say that I do not wish to waste the time of the house in replying to the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).
With the harmonious co-operation of the entire population of my riding of Brome-Missisquoi, as well as of every province, I am convinced that we shall be holding in 1967 genuine and sincere celebrations for the centennial of our great and young country.
We are indeed fortunate in not having among our people persons with the same frame of mind as the hon. member for Skeena.
I have often asked the Minister of Public Works questions concerning the world fair. From time to time, I noticed that in his replies, he never referred to the important things which were happening in Montreal.
A few weeks ago, the Prime Minister stated that he intended to appoint a permanent liaison officer to keep the federal government constantly and fully informed of the events in Montreal. As I say, not so many weeks ago, the minister told me that, for the time being, he was acting in that capacity himself.
In view of the speech he delivered and the announcement which the Prime Minister made, I hope the government will soon appoint a permanent liaison officer so that, from now on, we may get appropriate information on what is happening in Montreal, when we ask questions in the house.
Speaking in all sincerity, I submit that what we need at the present time is an efficient system permitting co-operation between the federal government, the provincial authorities of Quebec and those of the city of Montreal.

Mr. Chairman, if I may say so I think the best compliment I can pay to the last two speakers is to direct my remarks through you to the minister and say to him that my initial comments on this resolution were not made out of rancour or bitterness or anger; they were placed on the record because that was the way I felt about the situation after watching the progress, or lack of it, of the world fair in the months up to now. If hon. members want to get emotionally incensed about it and base their attitudes to this question on pure emotion rather than looking at it logically, that is their prerogative and I bear them no ill will whatsoever.

World Exhibition Corporation Act
With respect to the contention made earlier today and reiterated by the Leader of the Opposition that all the works done to date are illegal and without statutory sanction, I should like to tell the minister that I still hold this view. I believe the arguments which the hon. gentleman put forward in this regard do not hold water. He said, for instance, that the legislature of the province of Quebec brought Notre Dame island within the confines of the city of Montreal. That may well be, but that does not make Notre Dame island part of the island of Montreal, and the act specifically says that the world fair should be held on the island of Montreal.
The hon. gentleman indicated that not five cents has been spent by the federal government on the work which has been done up to the present moment. I do not think that argument has any validity with respect to whether what has been done has been done legally or not, because the relevant section of the act says quite clearly that there shall be held in Canada, on the island of Montreal, for six months, the exhibition referred to. The act does not talk about whether the federal government should spend money on the exhibition. That is immaterial.
The invitation cards which we received in August indicated that there was to be an official inauguration of the site. That is contrary to the law. The minister also said that the city of Montreal had until the end of 1964 to deliver the site; that is, to have it ready and available. This is immaterial too. We contend that the work which has been done up to this time has been illegal and contrary to the law of Canada, and we should all recognize this fact.
Even if this bill passes I do not think it will legalize what has been done up to now. However, I think there is a general disposition to agree that we should do something to regularize the illegal procedures which have been followed up to now. I still take the position that, so far, this has not been developed as an exhibition worthy of Canada in a national sense. So far, these activities have revolved primarily around the city of Montreal.

speechtext: The minister did not answer a couple of the questions that I put to him. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING NUMBER OF DIRECTORS, SALARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I have no comment to make.
The very fact that no comment was made accelerated the number of rumours in this regard, and I would ask the minister to direct his answer to this point.
The second question I asked him was this. How many countries to date have agreed to exhibit at the Canadian centennial exposition. My information may not be correct, but I have been informed that only two countries have expressed any direct interest in taking part in this exhibition. That is a very serious situation. The third question to which I did not receive an answer-it was brushed off-was what expenditure is to be made by the parliament of Canada? I am going to read from the remarks of the Prime Minister made in Montreal as reported on August 13.
In 1962, the federal government took the necessary action to establish the world fair corporation and to extend invitations to countries through our diplomatic channels abroad. It approved a contribution of up to $20 million to meet the direct costs of the exhibition.
Now the minister would have us believe that this $20 million was simply to be spent on a building or on a pavilion. Nothing of the sort. It represented the limit to which the former government would go in contributing to the direct costs of the exhibition, and that view was accepted by the present Prime Minister. Then the right hon. gentleman went on to say:
The federal government is also prepared to provide an exhibit which will be worthy of the country. It has undertaken to meet the very substantial additional costs that its engineers consider will be necessary to provide for the protection of this site against ice accumulation.
How much has been estimated as the cost which the federal government would accept in order to provide protection against ice accumulation? These various costs which I have mentioned will in themselves total something over $50 million. We want to know what the contribution is to be.
There is the building of the pavilion. Naturally there will be a national pavilion. But the undertaking of the government, when I was prime minister, was that our direct contribution would be no more than $20 million. Now the present government states there will be further costs in connection with the highway. I can recall the minister being asked a question as to the cost in this connection, and he said the highway would be built as part of the trans-Canada plan and the share paid by the federal government

would be the share normally paid by the federal government toward the cost of such highways.
I should like to get the outline of this expenditure. The direct contribution is $20 million. Then there is the pavilion. Over and above the pavilion, what further contribution is Canada to be asked to make? What is the estimated cost of providing protection against ice? What is the estimated cost of the road construction? What is the estimated cost of engaging additional engineers, and so on? We should know these things. There have been some grandiose plans suggested. As a matter of fact I notice someone has proposed that the parliament of Canada should provide free transportation for everyone who wants to go to the fair. I thought that was going a little far; indeed, I thought it was going much too far.
What I am trying to point out is that unless there is some degree of control there is no plan, however ephemeral or ridiculous, which might not ultimately be charged to the federal government. What degree of control do we have? What is the limit? I repeat that we said no more than $20 million was to be provided by way of direct assistance. That did not contemplate the cost of the pavilion. As soon as the minister gives us this information he will more or less have covered the picture.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to get some information from the minister. He himself mentioned the east-west Montreal expressway which will be built to help speed up traffic on the occasion of the world fair.
As he mentioned the subject, I would like to have some information concerning the laying out of that road, especially where it branches off from Dorchester boulevard. I understand, according to the lay-out, that the expressway is to start at a point west on Dorchester boulevard to reach Delorimier street, go up that street and from there continue east on Ontario street, up to the Bou-cherville tunnel. If I am right in this-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-I do not understand why the expressway would pass on an elevated road, in the eastern part of Montreal, on a very busy artery.
I should also like the minister to tell us what will be the responsibility of the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation concerning means of communication with and access to St. Helen's and Notre Dame islands, the site of the exhibition. At the official opening ceremony persided over by Mayor Drapeau, in spite of the roads now available, we certainly found ourselves in a serious traffic jam.
I wonder how we are going to have adequate means of access to the site, if the government, the city and the province do not decide immediately what are to be the roads of access and exit. I also wonder what comprehensive studies have been undertaken to prevent the exhibition from causing great big traffic jams which would jeopardize its success.

I wonder if the minister could get in touch with his colleague the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) to see whether the toll could be removed on Champlain bridge.
A member from the city of Montreal and myself urged that tolls be abolished on the Champlain bridge, as soon as possible, since even now that situation slows down traffic considerably in the city of Montreal because the work now going on on St. Helen's island and truck traffic are already causing quite serious bottlenecks on the roads between the south and the north shores.
I make this suggestion because I feel that the most important thing to think about after giving a structure, so to speak, to the corporation, is to ensure that all means of communication will benefit the world's fair.
Since the minister offers to amend the Canadian World Exhibition Act, I wonder whether he could tell us what are the intentions of the corporation about the pavilions which will be left there, once the fair is over. Rumours circulate to the effect that these pavilions could be sold to individuals. If such were the case, I think that we would be making a mistake because such a decision would lead to speculations with regard to the disposal of those pavilions.
In my opinion, these pavilions could be used to serve many purposes. I could even suggest to the minister that the corporation give up or sell some of them to the University of Montreal, which could use them as research centres, medical laboratories or even as hospitals.
As I mentioned already, these buildings could be used for many purposes, but I am of the opinion that before venturing too far, the minister should look after all the details to make sure, at the outset, that no speculation will be possible when the fair is over.
Mr. Chairman, I wish also to comment on some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) who, some time ago, seemed to blame the mayor of Montreal for the delays in the preparation of the world fair.
I feel the hon. member has been very badly informed, as in other circumstances, it may be added, because in the July 4, 1963 edition of La Presse, there was an article signed by Mr. Albert Tremblay to the effect that the city of Montreal was blaming Ottawa for the difficulties encountered in the preparation of the fair.
And the second paragraph of the article in question was as follows:
At a press conference called especially for that purpose, Messrs. Jean Drapeau and Lucien Saulnler defined once again the position of the administration-
World Exhibition Corporation Act
And the conclusion of the article was that the delay was due to a lack of decision on the part of the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that the Minister of Public Works should not be the only one blamed for that situation. I think that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is also responsible to a great extent for those delays for which I suggest there is no excuse, because of the short period at the disposal of the authorities of the city of Montreal to have the grounds ready.
I have a letter which the Prime Minister sent me on September 24, 1963 concerning the site of the exhibition, when I asked him to investigate the internal problems of the world exhibition corporation, particularly in connection with the resignation of Messrs. Carsley and Bienvenu. In his reply, the Prime Minister said then that a bill would soon be introduced in the house to amend the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation Act.
Mr. Chairman, I draw the attention of the house to the fact that this letter was dated September 24, 1963, and that it is only on December 20, that is nearly three months later, that the government finally introduced legislation to amend the said act.
I insist on calling this to the attention of the hon. member for Skeena and of the minister to stress the fact that the government is to be held responsible for the delays encountered in the decisions concerning the world fair.
Some time ago, I spoke of the reasons which motivated the resignation of Messrs. Carsley and Bienvenu. The minister did not reply. I would ask him to give those reasons to the house.
On August 22, 1963, La Presse published the letter which Mr. Bienvenu sent to the Prime Minister and copies of which he had given to the press. This is what he said in paragraph (b):
Important decisions were taken without the corporation being even invited to attend the discussions. There should not only be close coordination between the three levels of government but the commissioner should be provided with the means to ensure such co-ordination if senseless delays and duplication are to be avoided.
This letter is a clear indictment against the present government and the minister responsible for the world fair for their lack of co-ordination not to say co-operation. I wonder if the Liberal government should not assume part of the blame for those delays which nearly compromised the world fair, which, as we all hope, will be a success.
I hope, therefore, that the minister will not try to evade his share of responsibilities and will recognize that it is as late as eight months after the coming into power of his

World Exhibition Corporation Act party that entirely technical legislation is introduced in order to amend the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation Act. Indeed, the minister must admit that the amendments proposed only involve a very small part of the administrative structure and that they mostly concern the payment of allowances to the directors.
I feel that the government could have introduced much more practical amendments than those now before us and which only tend to amend the act so as to appoint two other directors and increase their remuneration.
I would like the minister to give us some definite explanation because his hesitation in making known the allowance to be paid to the commissioner general is absolutely unacceptable. I am wondering why the minister cannot tell us today what salary will be paid to this director who will soon be working for the company?
In this connection, I will give as an example the civil service commission. When this commission advertises a competition, the salary paid to the successful candidate is usually indicated. I cannot therefore understand why the Minister of Public Works is not in a position to tell us now what will be the salary paid to the commissioner general.
I realize that it may be advisable to take this decision when the house will be in recess, because we could then ask other information and I find that this perhaps is a characteristic attitude of the Minister of Public Works with his usual courtesy, he does not want to start a controversy.
I do not want to start a discussion on the matter, but I think we should insist, as members responsible for the money spent by the government, that the minister tell us how much the commissioner general will get.
I think it should be easy for the minister to answer that question. If one of his friends were to meet him and ask: "My dear minister, what is your salary?", it would be easy for him to answer his friend and it would not take him two months to do it, because he knows how much he is being paid. Therefore, I think the minister is in a position to tell us if the salary in question will amount to $10,000, $15,000, $25,000, $35,000 or even more than $35,000 or $50,000 per year.
It is important that we should get that information because we are asked to pass a measure meant precisely to give consideration to the matter of salaries to be paid to the directors of the world's fair.
I hope that the minister will answer the questions we put to him and, in particular,


will assure the house that neither the provincial nor the federal government will intervene from now on in the administration of the world's fair.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to start a debate but I know that some contracts were granted directly without public tenders being called. There might not have been anything wrong in that since the authorities of the city of Montreal are responsible for the preparation of the site but I hope that the three governments will give the corporation the independence it should have if we really want the fair to be a success.

Your Honour, when you were in the chair the other day, you ruled with respect to a previous question of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on December 10, and I want to quote briefly one of the paragraphs in your ruling as recorded at page 5666 of Hansard for December 10, where citation 355 of Beauchesne's fourth edition was quoted. It should be noted however that resolution is required not only when an amendment seeks to increase the amount previously approved by parliament, but also if it changes the modality and conditions of the grant authorized by the original legislation.
I submit that this bill seeks to change the modality and the conditions of the grant authorized by the original resolution with respect to the site of the fair itself, and no reference is in the resolution which the committee just considered to the site but only to increasing the number of directors of the corporation, to payments to the commissioner and the deputy commissioner, to establishing an executive committee of the board, to authorizing payment of remuneration by the corporation to directors, and to making further changes in connection with the administration of the act. The act at present states, and this has been mentioned quite a number of times:
In connection with the celebration of the centennial of confederaion in Canada in a manner in keeping with its national and historical significance, there shall be held in Canada, on the island of Montreal for a period of six months-
The bill now before us says:

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious, when venturing in such a field, where we have to approve or judge the true value of a design, we should abstain from rationalizing and stay within the artistic field.
I want to refer to the definition given to beauty appreciation by Saint Thomas, one of the greatest philosophers of all times. Here is how he defined it: Id quod visum aut auditum placet, which means "That which is seen and heard once is pleasing".
Then the appreciation comes from looking. The question is not to analyse, to rationalize, but merely to be aware that something seen or heard is agreeable.
If, like the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), we say: "Let


us look at it carefully and analyse it", we do an injustice, in my opinion, because I think such a work should not be judged.
Personally, I cannot say that at first sight the design pleased me and that I was under the impression that it was a work of art. On the other hand, other persons are under the impression, at first sight, that there is something beautiful in it, and this is why beauty in the field of such works is always comparative. One cannot judge this type of design in an absolute way, and that is why some will find it satisfactory, others will find it beautiful and others will say that there is nothing pleasant in all that.
If what we want is to get a design, a model or a crest such as this for the world fair, we should not start rationalizing and analysing all the details. People must be left with the idea of a thing which, seen once, may please. There is a symbol involved. It is somewhat like a piece of music which represents, now a river, then waterfalls. The question asked was:
Does Canada have a national emblem and, if so, what is the emblem?
The answer was:
Yes; three maple leaves conjoined on one stem.
This has been the law since November 21, 1921. I might add that a similar question was addressed to the previous government and a written answer was delivered, which never appeared in Hansard. But both the question and answer were identical. That is to say there would appear to be no difference of opinion legally respecting the assertion that Canada does have a national emblem which consists of three maple leaves conjoined on one stem.
This is no way unsympathetic to the province within which the fair is going to be held, because if we look at the base of the arms of the province of Quebec, the identifying symbolism for the province of Quebec is on a field or three maple leaves conjoined vert-that is to say, three green maple leaves on a gold base. Therefore there is a great deal of harmony between the symbolism of the province of Quebec and the symbolism of Canada. I would ask that those who are responsible would give some consideration to what has clearly been established law in Canada since the proclamation of November 21, 1921 during the time of the Borden administration.

Mr. Chairman, on some previous estimates a few hon. members were misinformed as to their opportunities to speak on the emergency measures organization. The minister later said that it would be all right during the estimates on the Department of Defence Production to speak about this subject. Have I a correct understanding of the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: I suggest this be done right away. If there are members who did wish to speak on the emergency measures organization and who have not done so by reason of our speed, I suggest they should speak right now.

As one who is interested in emergency measures, may I say it was not my intention to speak on the subject, but I do think the minister should say something about the changes which are taking place. The organization has been in a state of confusion for some time, and now that he has an opportunity of assessing the situation perhaps the hon. gentleman would wish to take this opportunity of clearing up a number of the doubts which have arisen. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by putting forward views which I have expressed in the past. However, there is some confusion in the minds of those who are

serving voluntarily in this field and the minister might help to clear this up by indicating the attitude which the government intends to take.

I do not intend to take up very much time on this item, but I promised certain people in my constituency who are interested in the emergency measures organization that I would say a few words about it. There can be no question that there is a lack of direction in the country with respect to this organization. Policies are being carried out which are now suspected of being obsolete and there has been a decline of interest in the organization in many quarters. I personally believe this organization will not be successful unless the training given to members includes training to deal with disasters of all types. I think training of this type would interest a great many people, including possibly those who feel that there is no adequate defence against an attack by nuclear weapons.
In this connection I should like to read from an article which appeared in the Financial Post of October 19. The heading is: "If the Big Bomb drops, can EMO Cope?" and there is a further heading which says: "The harsh truth is that it can't".
This poses some difficult questions for Drury and his advisers:
There is the over-all policy question: should EMO still be formally oriented toward nuclear war or should it now be officially aimed toward natural disaster work?
Although much of the work that has to be carried out serves both purposes anyway, a rethinking of the main direction of civil defence w-ouldn't mean scrapping all-or even most-of the existing structure.
But there are still purely "nuclear" programs underway. For example, Ottawa and the provinces spent $602,500 in the last fiscal year on radioactivity measuring instruments. These would be useful to tell the public when radioactivity was reaching dangerous levels, but if the public has nowhere to go to get away from it, does it gain much by knowing?
Should Ottawa go on urging Canadians to build fall-out shelters?
Some people here are still being urged to build them though Great Britain gave up this policy two years ago. The article goes on:
If the Berlin wall and the Cuban blockage couldn't get the Canadian public digging, what hope is there now?
Drury has other heavy responsibilities-the new Department of Industry, Defence Production, government research and five crown corporations- and hasn't had much time to tackle these civil defence questions. He was to begin a detailed policy examination this week.
Whether it will lead to any basic changes remains to be seen. But one thing is certain: thanks to the threat of nuclear war, Canadians are now better prepared than ever to look after themselves in any local or national emergency. It is a happy side advantage from an unhappy era.
I do not intend to speak at any length on this subject. But I would bring to the attention

of the minister the fact that there is a great deal of uncertainty about this program. It is too late in the session to deal with the question in any detail but we hope the minister will turn his attention to this matter and give direction to the Canadian people who are interested in this work, so that they may get some leadership along the lines suggested in the article from which I have quoted.
Does the minister intend to explain what the government's intentions are?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
If there is no one else to speak on this item, perhaps I might say, very briefly, that the purpose and function of the emergency measures organization are closely linked with defence policy. The committee is fully aware that the whole of our defence policy is currently under review. This organization is its corollary. The two are proceeding hand in hand. It would be my hope that about the time that there is, in the new year, a new formulation of defence policy there will be, to the extent necessary, a new formulation of the EMO approach.
I am in full agreement with the remarks of the hon. member who suggested there should be a duality of purpose in the approach of the emergency measures organization-that the organization should be prepared to cope not only with nuclear disaster but with natural disasters. This is a consideration which is being borne in mind in the review which is currently taking place.
