Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to make the kind of speech I ordinarily would make if it were not so late in the session. I should have liked, for example, to discuss in some considerable detail some of the things which I feel need doing very badly with regard to the problem of Indians.
6236	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I must say it is very difficult to be critical of the minister because he has made some very fine speeches, very liberal, with a small "1", and he has not only made good speeches but, in addition, when members, and I include myself, have gone to him with particular problems he has shown a very deep interest and a sympathetic approach. However, when it comes to the problems of the Indians it seems to me we have a very long way to go.
I want to give one illustration of the kind of thing which I think needs to be done. I put some questions on the order paper recently with regard to the efforts of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources to foster co-operatives for the Eskimos and similar questions with regard to the efforts of this department in the fostering of co-operatives for Indians. If the minister will take the time when the house adjourns to look at the answers, he will see precisely what I mean. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has specifically assigned two or three people to work full time on this matter actively and aggressively, with the result that there are 14 or 15 very active and successful co-operatives among the Eskimos of northern Canada. But the answers I got with regard to the support of co-operatives for Indians would indicate there is nobody working full time on this job in the minister's department, and that anything which is done is largely done through the efforts of provincial departments, and that if there is any success it is almost incidental to a large extent.
If we are really thinking in terms of solving the Indian problem we must think not of giving them welfare but rather of getting them to be able to function on their own. I can think of no better way of getting them to function on their own than to form cooperatives, both producer and consumer, where they will be responsible to themselves and will look after themselves instead of waiting for the department or the church or the Hudson's Bay Company or some other organization to do it for them. Without going further today, into the problem of the Indians, I suggest to the minister that he should look at this matter very seriously.
I should also like to say a few words about the question of citizenship. Here again I must say I am more than satisfied with the specific responses I have had from the minister with regard to actual cases. But it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if the minister has to solve a case himself there is an admission right away that we have failed because the standards should be so clear and simple that these cases should be solved before they get to the minister. The minister has said that he is reviewing the standards, and I hope
[Mr. Orllkow.i
he will continue to be the minister long enough to be able to solve this problem and lay down policies and standards much more suited to the 60's before he leaves for another job. The revision of the standards for citizenship is long overdue.
I am one of those people who believe that the democratic system of society under which we supposedly live is the best system we can have. If this is so, it seems to me we should not worry too much whether or not a few people who have some doubts about citizenship and our democratic way of life receive citizenship. I know, and I am sure the minister knows better than I do, that in every city in Canada where there are ethnic groups, non-French, non-Anglo-Saxon, some of these people having come here before world war I, there are hundreds if not thousands of people who have not been able to get their citizenship. I have in mind Ukrainians in Winnipeg and probably Finns in Port Arthur. I could go down the list in each area where there are people of the various ethnic groups.
The answer up till now has been that these people are members of the communist party or members of organizations which have been classified as being sympathetic to the communist party. I hold no brief for the political views of these people. I have fought the communists at every turn over the years. In my constituency there are probably as many as in any other constituency in Canada, and I have fought them all my life. At the same time, however, if in 1963 we refuse to grant the right to become citizens to persons who have lived in Canada since 1915 or 1920 simply because they are, or are supposed to be, communists it seems to me we have not got very much confidence in our democratic way of life. It seems to me that if the minister is going to look at the standards of citizenship, then this is something at which he should look very seriously.
There is one more point I should like to make, Mr. Chairman. In recent years a number of people from the United States have come to Canada. Many of these people are highly qualified in various fields, such as science, town planning, and what have you. They have been appointed to some very responsible positions in Canada. I can think of one whose name I shall mention because he has been referred to in the press, namely Mr. Blomenthal of the city of Toronto, who has been the chief town planner of that city. I can think of several who are scientists who have represented Canadian organizations within the fields in which they are working at various international scientific conferences. We thought enough of their abilities and their

qualifications to let them come into Canada. They are holding responsible jobs. I think of one who is doing work that the government of Canada thought so important they erected a building costing a couple of million dollars in which he could work. Some of these people have applied for citizenship and have been turned down. I can think of nothing more stupid, nothing which indicates more to me that we really have not got confidence that our democratic society will work, than this action. If we had that confidence, we certainly would not turn down citizen applications from people like these. I think the minister should have a careful look at this situation after the house adjourns and he has the time to do so. Many of these cases have been on his desk for some time.
I should like to say a few words on immigration. I was glad to hear the minister say that the government intends to follow a more aggressive policy than it has. I was glad to hear the minister say that his objective for the next year is to have more than 100,000 immigrants come to Canada. There will be general agreement with this policy amongst the population. The labour movement of Canada, for obvious reasons, has been skeptical of a policy of mass immigration. After all, when you have 500,000 or 750,000 people unemployed, the trade unions that were formed to protect the conditions and way of life of their members cannot be blamed if they are a little worried. They have made it very clear, however, that they support increased and continuing immigration into Canada, provided we keep in mind the problem of unemployment.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, they have also made it very clear, and they did this as early as 1957, that they are completely opposed to the discriminatory immigration policies of past governments on the basis of race, religion and colour. I should like to quote a couple of sentences from their submission to the government in October, 1957. This is the submission of the Canadian Labour Congress and reads in part as follows:
The present Immigration Act is thoroughly unsatisfactory. It was passed without giving anyone but a few government departments and the transportation companies any opportunities to be heard. It contains a series of provisions which are a threat to civil liberties which the British people fought for centuries to establish. It enshrines the vicious principle of racial discrimination. It gives the administration sweeping and arbitrary powers, with a minimum of judicial control. It has been administered in a high-handed spirit which has often totally disregarded elementary human rights. Immigration officials overseas have often been imperfectly informed of conditions in Canada, and have accordingly misinformed intending immigrants, and induced people to come here at times when it would have been better if they had stayed at home.

The Prime Minister and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration have been making speeches in which they try to create the impression that Canada's immigration policies have been shorn of their discriminatory and racialist slant. Thus the Prime Minister said in parliament on October 18, 1963:
-I should like to make it clear that the present government, like its predecessor, is firmly opposed in principle and in practice to racial discrimination.
He said that, Mr. Chairman, when he was asked a question about the refusal of the United States government to permit Mr. Wayson S. Choy, a Canadian citizen, entry to the United States. This is a very laudable statement of intent, but it does not really fit the Canadian situation. If we examine the Canadian Immigration Act, and more particularly the regulations which have been promulgated by the department over the years supposedly to carry out the intent of the act, we can see how far we have strayed from this very fine statement of principle which the Prime Minister expressed on October 18.
Permanent admission to Canada is regulated by the Immigration Act. There are a whole series of prohibited classes, including of course people who have been convicted of certain criminal offences, people with communicable diseases, people who have been guilty of having subversive associations, etc. Section 5 of the Immigration Act lists classes of persons prohibited from entering Canada. Subsection 1 of this section prohibits members of subversive organizations from entering Canada. Under this section any person who has, while living in a country behind the iron curtain, attended a university can and probably will be prohibited from immigrating to Canada since in all likelihood membership in the young communist league of that country was probably a requirement of university attendance. It seems to me that this provision is completely unnecessary.
Section 5, paragraph (t) prohibits the entry into Canada of persons who cannot or do not fulfil or comply with any of the conditions or requirements of this act, or the regulations, or any orders lawfully made or given under this act or the regulations. This section, gives unlimited power to the officials of this department to refuse entry into Canada to anybody on any ground or without any ground because the decision rests entirely on the whim of the departmental officials. I am not saying they use this section, but the fact it is there gives them unlimited power which I think is an unnecessary power in a democratic society.

Now, the main control on the admission of immigrants to Canada is based upon regulations passed by the cabinet, under the authority of the act. These regulations can, of course, be changed more readily than the act itself. Under these regulations, Mr. Chairman, we make it much more difficult, in fact we make it virtually impossible, for people from Asia and Africa to come into Canada. Certainly, it is much more difficult for them than for people in other parts of the world. In other words, what we have done has been to apply the principle that George Orwell talked about in his book "Animal Farm", when he said, "All pigs are equal but some are more equal than others." We have said that all people are equal but some are more equal than others.
Section 61 of the Immigration Act, which deals with the regulations which may be made by the governor in council, permits,
(g) the prohibiting or limiting of admission of persons by reason of
(i)	nationality, citizenship, ethnic group, occupation, class or geographical area of origin.
(ii)	peculiar customs, habits, modes of life or methods of holding property,
(iii)	unsuitability having regard to the climatic, economic, social, industrial, educational, labour, health or other condition or requirements existing, temporarily or otherwise, in Canada or in the area or country from or through which such person comes to Canada,
(iv)	probable inability to become readily assimilated or to assume the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship within a reasonable time after their admission.
Mr. Chairman, if there is any way in which the department could find an excuse to keep a person out other than those listed here, I certainly cannot think of one. In this section you are talking about things such as customs, habits, climatic conditions, and so on, and of course if the people in the department think the number of non-white people in Canada is as large as they want it, they could-they have done this in other years, although I do not say it is done now-take the attitude that people from the West Indies, for example, ought not to come here because the climate of Canada is cold-it is certainly cold today-and therefore these people would not fit into our country.
It seems to me that the time to stop this nonsense has long passed, and I think the minister should really get at it. I think these kind of racial and religious prejudices should have long since been eliminated in Canada. Under section 31 of the regulations with respect to the Immigration Act, which deals with handling requirements and specifies the type of classes permitted to enter Canada, subsection (d) says that the following may enter:
[Mr. Orlikow.l

A person who is a citizen of any country of Europe, including Turkey; of any country of North, Central or South America or islands adjacent thereto, or Egypt, Greece or Lebanon-
In other words this regulation can be used to bar people from every country in Africa and every country in Asia but Turkey, Egypt, Lebanon and Israel. How much more discriminatory could we get, even if we tried harder? I think it is time the government made public a statement of policy showing clearly what the government, rather than the officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, consider to be necessary standards of training for admission to Canada and what sort of economic circumstances in Canada are required when the number of immigrants to be permitted to enter Canada is decided.
Parliament contemplated giving an applicant a hearing by a special inquiry officer. If that officer found a person was not admissible, that person should have the right of appeal. But the regulations have now been expanded to say that a person can have a hearing only as to whether or not he has a visa. If the department officials think a person undesirable, they do not have a hearing on the reasons for that person being excluded. They have a hearing only on whether the person has a visa, which the department has already refused to grant. Thus they never discuss the real reasons for exclusion. Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, the supreme court has upheld this right of the department. It seems to me that the immigration appeal board, which is now composed of former or actual immigration officials, should be completely and totally divorced from the department. It should be required by the act or the regulations to give reasons for its judgments, and should have authority to make recommendations to the minister.
Further, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that prospective immigrants should have the right to appeal and also the right to be told why they are being turned down. They certainly do not have this right at the present time. These are just a few of the things which I think the minister should look into. I hope he will have a chance to look into them before he leaves this department, if he does, because I think if before the house meets to discuss the estimates in the next session the minister changes the regulations and recommends changes to the act, it will please members of the house, certainly those in this group, and I think it will please most of the people in Canada.

Over the years I have been interested in the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and it can be agreed that slowly but surely we have been making many improvements in this very important area of Canadian activity.
I was pleased to hear the minister indicate that he will continue and expand the new humanitarian emphasis that in recent years appeared in relation to immigration matters, and that he hopes the target of 100,000 newcomers will be reached in the next fiscal year.
There has been an improvement in the attitude of Canadians generally towards immigration matters, resulting from a combination of circumstances, such as the activities of the United Nations organizations operating in this field, and the voluntary groups that have carried out extensive adult education programs among Canadians. I refer in particular to the work of the Canadian citizenship
6240	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration council which has branches in every part of the country and has an adult education program as one of its main functions, interesting Canadians in improving the immigration laws, and their attitude toward Canadian citizenship.
It will be agreed that the changes introduced in the regulations in February, 1962, were a step forward. One of the complaints hon. members had concerning the regulations was their attempt to define qualifications for intending immigrants for the purpose of maintaining what might be described as an elusive ethnic balance. To me this always had some element or overtones of discrimination, and the new regulations, placing the emphasis on skills and training rather than on conforming to an indefinable ethnic balance, are a much fairer approach.
Another improvement in the regulations was the inclusion of unsponsored immigrants. The element of sponsorship was restricted to a very narrow group, or rather I should say unsponsored immigrants, and this narrow group mainly included the old commonwealth countries and the western European countries. This meant that, with the improving standards of living in Europe and the United Kingdom, the traditional sources for large numbers of new citizens were rapidly drying up. Prior to the regulations being changed in 1962 there had been a declining inflow of immigrants from those traditional sources, and I would presume that it is largely because of the changes in the regulations that we can now anticipate the increase that was mentioned by the minister. As a matter of fact there was an encouraging increase last year.
Before I leave this point I would like to say there has been a tendency to be more restrictive on applications for intended immigrants from Greece than from other similar parts of Europe. I have found, in my own personal experience, it has always been more difficult to get approval, particularly for unsponsored immigrants, from Greece than from other countries of Europe located in the same area.
I wonder if the minister could indicate to us to what degree the change in the regulations has resulted in the increase of immigrants. Is it possible to separate numerically the improved immigration figures on the basis of the broader approach taken by the amendments to the regulations in 1962?
I was also pleased to see there has been a tendency, along these same humanitarian lines, towards encouraging the reunion of family groups. Again this is due to the broadened regulations. Before they were changed they were so narrow in their application to


Chinese immigrants as to be almost prohibitive. If I wished to be sensational I could relate many tragic experiences of Chinese Canadians during the early '50's when it was impossible for them to bring their wives or married children over to this country, due to the very restrictive nature of the regulations.
I am also pleased to note that the minister will proceed to amend the act as quickly as possible. As I have already indicated, it is one thing to amend the regulations; but regulations must be reinforced by specific legislation, and I am sure that the minister will be assured of support from all sides of the house when he moves to bring the Immigration Act into line with the more humane approach which has developed in Canada, and in the world generally, toward these matters.
I should like to say a word in the area of the minister's other responsibilities, concerning the superintendent general of Indian affairs, and I will be brief owing to the shortage of time. I am pleased to see that here too there has been a tremendous improvement in the attitude of members of this house, and of the Canadian public generally, in respect to the rights of our first citizens. The Canadian Indian, if we look back in historic perspective, has been subject to segregation, neglect and discrimination in every respect. From time to time sensational situations develop which bring to the attention of the public some of the extreme problems in looking after the welfare of these, our first citizens. I recall it was just a year ago when Manitoba was exposed to a rather sensational amount of publicity regarding a situation which developed in one of the reservations in northern Manitoba. If the searchlight of publicity had been applied at the same time to any of the other reservations, I am sure a similar situation would have been exposed. However, since the unlimited franchise was extended to the Indian population of Canada-this is also a recent occurrence; I believe in 1960-politicians have become interested. We have had more discussion in this house concerning Indian affairs than ever before. The Indians themselves have become interested in public affairs. I have noticed this in my constituency, in which there are two reservations. It is now possible to hold regular public meetings in which the residents of the reservations take a very keen and active interest. But I think even more encouraging has been the expansion of interest to neighbouring communities. Segregation, out of sight, out of mind, has been the great curse of our Indian problem. The fact that these our first citizens were isolated

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
on reservations kept the problems largely hidden from the population generally.
I want to encourage the minister and the department along the lines of the encouragement already given to voluntary groups which are now appearing in communities right across Canada. I believe financial assistance is available to friendship societies, for example, where they are formally organized and make application to the department for such assistance. I am wondering whether it is possible to get some idea of the number of friendship groups or societies which have qualified for the available grants. Here at long last is an attempt being made on the part of Canadians generally to make contact with the people on the reserves, to introduce them to the community, and in turn to have regular contacts and associations with the Indians in their own reservations. It seems to me that this is the best way to deal with a problem which has been with us for far too long.
With regard to education, again we are moving forward. The program of integration of students in our community schools has, I think, been the most progressive approach to this problem in recent times. In the past four or five years in which it has been in operation I have seen the schoolchildren in the reservations of my own constituency almost entirely removed from this double situation of segregation-educational segregation as well as ethnic segregation-and fitted in happily with the schools in the surrounding communities. There have been expressions of approval not only by the Indian population themselves but also by people who for the first time are having Indian children to their homes-because some of these youngsters are boarded-during the Christmas recess, and making important contacts in this way.
Another major difficulty with our first citizens is the economic problem. Here is one area in which we have not made much progress. I know there are special placement officers who have been appointed who are beginning to do outstanding work; but if we are really going to tackle the problems of our first citizens which are so well known, next to the educational solutions we must have some kind of program which will make it possible for them to find suitable and adequate economic means of supporting themselves.
I am sure the minister agrees that the ultimate objective in all these programs is to move the Indian population toward full citizenship as quickly as possible. As a former minister of northern affairs I know this was my objective with the Canadian Eskimo; while there are some differences of approach
to the problem here, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North indicated, I know there is general unanimity in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, as well as in the department of northern affairs, to move these first Canadians toward full citizenship as quickly as possible. This can be accomplished only as the concept of community development pioneered by my native province of Manitoba in recent years is accepted in each provincial area. Until we can develop a spirit, a self-propelling spirit, in each of the Indian reservations which gives them the motivation and creativity to come to grips with their own problems, we are not going to make it possible for these first citizens to become real first citizens in fact as well as in name.

Mr. Chairman, since immigration is a vital matter, I apologize for having to take the time of the committee to make some brief remarks.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to offer my heartfelt congratulations to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau) for the stirring speech he delivered a few days ago in Quebec city. Should he also be congratulated for his tactful blame of the Quebec provincial authorities?
Indeed, immigration is an extremely important and even crucial matter if one considers, for instance, that from 1951 to 1961 the population of Canada increased by
4.230.000	and that 25 per cent of that increase must be ascribed to immigration.
I should like to submit to the house a few figures I compiled; they go back to 1926. I hope I will be able one of these days to go as far back as 1867.
At any rate, those figures indicate that 3,102,449 immigrants were admitted to Canada between 1926 and 1962. Mr. Chairman, I do not mean to be aggressive or spiteful but I should like to point out that these figures indicate that there is a real threat to French Canada. Only 90,206 of those immigrants were French speaking and, by that, I mean specifically French speaking people like Belgians and Frenchmen. On the other hand, immigrants of Anglo-Saxon origin, that is the English, the Scots and the Irish, totalled 1,038,888.
Mr. Chairman, the difference in numbers is fantastic. I am not saying that all of the
3.102.000	immigrants were English speaking but I wonder if the Department of Citizenship and Immigration could make a special effort to translate into practice the principle of biethnism we hear so much about.
Messrs. Laurendeau and Dunton may well indulge in semantics to define the words

Mr. Chairman, I welcome to our fine and great country people from the British isles and elsewhere. Everybody is welcome as far as I am concerned.
We want to create a Canadian ideal based on the fundamental respect of the rights of the two great races of which we are proud.
Mr. Chairman, let us not, therefore, hand to the extremists of our country a weapon they try to use to their advantage, especially in the province of Quebec, where there are bad Canadians who want to break up confederation. We, the Liberals of the province of Quebec, are trying to prevent this because we want to maintain confederation as radiant as possible.
In order to do so, however, it is essential that the decrease in population among French speaking Canadians, which has taken alarming proportions according to the figures I have just quoted, should be stopped.
Consequently, I earnestly ask and I even beg the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to make a firm and continued effort to redress that difference which has worked against French Canadians. I suggest that if 25 per 100 of the increase in population from 1951 to 1961 is due to immigration, a good and a sound immigration policy can help to save confederation.

Many things have come up in the debate, including the contribution of the hon. member who has just spoken, that I should like to get into. My disappointment is most bitter in connection with the fact that I have a great number of Indian problems. I think I represent as many Indians as anyone in this house, between six and seven thousand; no one is sure of the number. Honestly, they are in the most pitiful condition of probably any inhabitants of Canada, and there are a great number of questions to ask and remarks I should like to make in connection with them, but I will give them over in the main and stick to questions.
Before I do, I would remind the minister of the remarks made by my hon. friend from Timiskaming, and the need to investigate the orders in council in that situation. I want to be even more specific and blunt than the hon. member for Timiskaming. I do not know whether the minister is aware, but this is what he was suggesting, that a number of members of parliament in the past have worked on this kind of case and have used their influence to smooth this kind of arrangement. What we would be interested in knowing is that this practice has been stopped
[Mr. Choquette.l
by this government, and that there is no possibility of this being an avenue for the kind of private patronage available to any member of parliament. If the minister would like some names of members of parliament from previous parliaments and would like to see the record checked in this regard, I will be glad to provide him with three or four.
I should like to ask the minister one question with reference to immigration. It relates to the fact that for a number of years-

Is the hon. member suggesting that a member of parliament should not intervene on behalf of the constituents who are having difficulties with respect to immigration or citizenship? Perhaps he would tell us just what he means.

I have got all kinds of letters here where I have intervened. I am referring to the situation where certain members of parliament have acted as a regular channel over the years. In most cases they are lawyers, and there has been a fee exchanged. That is what I am referring to. It is something distinct and special and, I think, a bad situation.
I should like to point out to the minister that there has been a great big holdback in the coming to Canada of Italian people who have qualified. As a matter of fact, I think three years ago there were some 59,000 people who had qualified to come to Canada and who were being held up. I have a large Italian population in my riding. This pressure is upon me all the time. The minister has told us that the Italians who come to this country are very seldom involved in crime, relatively speaking, and that they have a great sense of inner responsibility. This is one of the reasons why a lot more of these people could be brought into this country as a responsibility of their relatives. Instead, what seems to be the situation is that the demands which are being made on relatives in terms of bank accounts, housing facilities and requirements such as that have been increased in the last year or two, rather than decreased, and I would like to know from the minister on his estimates what the holdback figure is at the present time and whether it has been much reduced.

Mr. Chairman, just before the break I was talking about the question of Italian immigration. I should like to add that I believe it is time for our government to talk firmly, directly and brutally to the Italian government about the fact that it is so difficult for Italians with any techniques or training or skills to get out of Italy to come to Canada. Very many of them are now going to Germany, France and the other common market countries. There is a very large flow there, but I think the minister and his officials will have to admit that there is a tendency on the part of the Italian government and officials to block off this kind of skilled person coming to Canada and, of course, there is encouragement on the part of the Italian government for unskilled people to come to Canada. I think we can absorb a good many of the unskilled. We have and they have made their way and have risen very well, particularly in the business world, the construction world and in carpentry. I do not know where our construction industry would be today if it were not for the Italians and the contribution they have made.
But I suggest we need to talk very directly to Italy in this regard because it seems to me this is one country where we can get many more people. With reference to the argument of the hon. member for Lotbiniere about wanting a greater Canada and recognizing that it is people who will bring this about, if it is hard to get people from France and Belgium of French speaking background, perhaps there is an affinity between the Italians and the French that would make Italy promising ground for the kind of recruiting efforts that the minister suggested the Quebec government should undertake.
There is one last point in connection with immigration on which I want to touch and that is the possibility of an amnesty for more than just the Chinese people who entered Canada illegally. I have spoken to the minister about this matter. In my own riding I am acquainted with five or six people who happen to be Portuguese and who are not here on forged passports but are here illegally, in that they came in on visas, although the visas were not forged. At the present time they are working in the country. I have talked to several of them. I am not trying to condone the fact that they are breaking the law. They have told me that to their knowledge there are probably 500 or 600 people of their particular background in northern Ontario in the ring extending from the lakehead around to Sudbury.
Most of these people have been able to carry on for three, four or five years in this country because they are good, steady workmen who are never in trouble. It seems to me that some kind of effort is merited not only to examine and clear up each one of these cases that are outstanding, but also if they are typical of other groups of people of other backgrounds who are in this country illegally I think an over-all amnesty that would give them a chance to come forward with some hope of being able to stay here would be a very good move. I hope the minister will consider this. I think it should be much wider than just for the Chinese because people from other lands are involved.
Turning to the Indian affairs branch, I received a very sad document the other day from the Little Longlac chamber of commerce, a very prosperous small town in northern Ontario. It is supported by the Kimberly-Clark Corporation, one of the most enlightened companies I have had any dealings with. Right adjacent to this community there is an Indian reserve and the Little Longlac chamber of commerce points out in its representations, which went to the minister and to the Prime Minister, that there is a desperate situation in the community. You can see it in the statistics that half a dozen of the Indians from the reserve adjacent to this community have been killed on the roads or have died terrible deaths in other ways in the last few years as a result of drinking, careless behaviour, a complete misunderstanding of traffic rules and such things. Little Longlac or Macdiarmid in my constituency are perfect examples to show how badly we have done with the northern Ontario Indians.
I know the minister is sympathetic in this regard. I assume he was the one who was responsible for sending to us this pamphlet, "The Dilemma for Our Indian People", by James P. Mulvihill, O.M.I. I think it is an
6244	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration excellent analysis of the situation. It is quite apparent that we need to do something drastic. As far as I can see, in the northern Ontario Indians we have a form of crisis on our hands. It is no good belabouring the Indians affairs branch. Many of their agents have behaved like feudal barons, but they have not had any background or training in sociology or social work. It seems to me that many of them behave as though they are carrying out a routine job and are taking the easiest way out of it. But I think the reason for this is our lack of response. The Indians now have the vote, but as you go around an area the size of mine, which I would point out to hon. members comprises almost one third of the area of Ontario, you begin to appreciate that there is no simple answer.
I am sick about the situation of the Indians in my area. I have talked to the Jesuits, who have a religious interest in many of the reserves, and they are sick at heart about the situation. Many of them are despondent. I talked to one old priest last year just before he died. He had a total of approximately $7,000 in i.o.u.'s in a great big box in his kitchen. These were i.o.u.'s that had been given for two or three dollars at a time by Indians on his reserve so they could make a phone call, buy bread or use the money for taxi fare to go to the unemployment insurance office. He had no complaint about the fact he had advanced this form of charity. He knew it was charity. He knew the i.o.u.'s did not mean anything, but to him they were typical of the fact that these people always had to be turning to him or to someone else for assistance, even for a minor loan of $2 in order to go down the road a way.
This kind of difficulty is widespread throughout my whole riding. Every Indian reserve of which I know in my riding has a water problem. For example, at Heron Bay they have three pumps, and wells have been sunk. None of the Indians want to use any of the wells. They have a real complaint. Traditionally, they use the river, and the river is full of pulpwood for most of the year. We have been trying to do something about this. Gull Bay has had some wells sunk and some pumps put in. Every time I go there the Indians tell me that the pumps are not working. Sometimes this is the result of vandalism and sometimes it is recalcitrance on their part to use the facilities or take care of them.
I can give the minister a typical example. I went into one place last spring on the Gull Bay Indian reserve and a young man pointed to the walls. He said, how would you expect anybody to live through a winter in

this place. He and his wife had just been through the winter. You could see outside and there were the remains of some snow on the ground. You could see right through the walls. I was quite incensed, so I went to the Indian agent. I discovered that the Indian affairs branch had provided him with liner for his shack, provided insulation and everything. It had been brought up by trucks, and as soon as it landed he had sold it. Then, he and his wife had gone on a drunk and left the kids to be looked after by the grandmother.
I could tell the committee a really sad story. Last summer a 17 year old girl came to me and wanted to know if there was any possibility of getting a job. Obviously, she was pregnant. I made inquiries and discovered she was seven months pregnant. She was a very pretty girl. I inquired into the case from both the people on the reserve and the Indian agent, as well as from people who did welfare work. Here was a little girl who, at 13, was dragged off into the woods by one of the older Indians and kept as a prisoner for six months. None of the other Indians told on him. Finally, a school teacher found out about it and got the police. This man wound up with three or four years in Stoney Mountain and the poor girl was a physical wreck. She had been beaten and battered, and she wound up in a training school. She came out of the training school at 15, and where did she go? She hit the streets of Port Arthur. I do not know what can be done with a child like that. She does not know who her father was, and she does not know the potential father of the child she was carrying.
If this were just an isolated situation, if this were just the odd case, I could say we just needed mild remedial measures. However, that is not the situation. The minister can go into almost any reserve within range of the highway, and the tracks, where the white men are living close to the Indians, and this will be the kind of situation he will find. I went into one Indian home near Armstrong in my riding a little over a year ago and talked to the Indian father. He stated his daughter was home from school. She had gone to grade 12 and she hoped she would go on to be a nurse. I said, you must feel very proud. He said that he did, but she was not going to be a nurse. I asked why and he said she was pregnant. I asked how this happened. He told me she came home during the summer holiday and there was a pretty wild crowd around there. There happened to be some troops in the vicinity and that was the end of another promising Indian career.

I do not want to suggest any scandal. However, the actual living conditions, the morality, the behaviour of the Indians in my area of northwestern Ontario, including the riding of Kenora-Rainy River, all the way along the railway is as bad as this.
What have we got in the Indian affairs branch to face up to this situation? So far as I know, in that whole area we have one training or location office. To my knowledge, there is not any person intimately connected with Indian affairs in that region who is a trained social worker. The Indian agency centre for our area is in the town of North Bay, which is a long distance from the concentration of Indians in our part of the country.
I want to put it to the minister that it is about time there was a serious effort made in that region along the north shore, and up to Hudson bay, to bring to bear the skills that are available in the Indian affairs branch to do something for these people. Obviously, the solution is not a religious one, although I believe the religious authorities could help. I am sure they will help, and they are ready to help. It is more than just a community problem of association with whites in the small towns around which the Indians cluster. It is more than just an employment problem, although the fact is that employment is a factor. I know of one reserve on which there were 112 able-bodied men right in the middle of a timber limit that is being exploited by one of the big companies in Canada. However, only two men out of the whole band of 112 who were considered adult and ablebodied had any kind of permanent employment. You look at the figures for forest land in Ontario held by or for the Indians, and it is pitifully small. It is down to a few thousand square miles for the whole province of Ontario.
I can express my umbrage and my dissatisfaction. I have not any simple answer to suggest. It puzzles me, it defeats me, it discourages me. All I do know is that it will take some of the best wisdom and some of the largest resources that we can muster in terms of money and skill to really arrest the situation and to begin to convert these Indians into people of whom we can be proud, as Canadians, instead of being ashamed that these people live as they do. Some people are saying that the minister is going on to bigger things. I hope if that is his ambition he does. However, I suggest there is no bigger disgrace that we have to face as Canadians than the Indian situation-I can only speak of northern Ontario. I cannot think of any greater challenge for the minister or his successor than to really do something about
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration this situation-instead of just what I am doing, standing up and talking about it.
I should like to close by saying that I think within the Indian affairs branch there is a group of people who are waiting for the kind of imagination and leadership to gear and move this kind of program. However, it has to be much more intensive than before. There has to be more encouragement from the minister and from the senior officials of the department than I think has been given. I suggest that we have one experiment going in my area. A gentleman in Port Arthur who is working for the children's aid has taken on one of the reserves, one of those where conditions are poor. As a result of the cooperation he has had from the Indian affairs branch, he is carrying out a recreational program that is a real bootstrap operation. I should like to suggest to the minister that needs to be examined very soon to see if the results are worth while. If they are, this type of program should be applied to other reserves in the area.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have been longer than I intended in making these remarks. I should like to conclude now by saying that my sense of shame that my constituents have to live this way and be isolated as they are with a kind of apartheid with which most of us go along, although we would never accept it as a philosophy, has caused me to speak. I will tell the minister that any move he makes in this regard that shows an awareness of the problem and an attempt to meet it will have my support. I can almost guarantee, too, that he will not have to stand up in this house and plead or beg for money, or for votes to support it.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few subjects I would like to talk about on the estimates of this department. The first has to do with Indians and Eskimos. One might ask, what have I to do with Indians and Eskimos, since I represent primarily an urban riding in which there are no Indian reservations. But there is located within the riding of Edmonton West the largest Indian and Eskimo hospital in the country. This is the first subject I would like to draw to the attention of the minister. The Charles Camsell hospital does not come under his direct jurisdiction, but under that of his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare; but this hospital deals with the people in whom the minister is primarily interested, as is the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I know the northern health services came under the examination of the Glassco commission, and one of the recommendations was that the Charles Camsell hospital be not rebuilt. I happen to know a

6246	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration number of the doctors who were on the project team, shall we say, that looked into this matter and I had rather violent disagreements with them in this regard. With all due respect to these gentlemen, I think they were at least one generation ahead of their time with regard to medical services for our Indian and Eskimo populations, particularly as they deal with the Northwest Territories and the province of Alberta.
It was only a few years ago that the Indian and the Eskimo was prepared to accept and trust the white man's medicine. We now know from statistics that the health condition of our reserve Indians and our Indians and Eskimos in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon has improved immeasurably. But this progress must be maintained. There is a tremendous amount of work to be done in this regard. We can help by encouraging them to continue coming to a hospital where they are welcome, where they feel they are among people of their own kind, where the staff know how to handle them. An Indian or Eskimo patient from the Northwest Territories is not the same as the white man off the streets of the city of Edmonton.
I must confess that I was absolutely astounded at the philosophy that seemed to be propounded by those advocating that the Charles Camsell hospital be not rebuilt or modernized, because the main building is an old college building going back 50 or 60 years, and the remaining portion is a redwood building erected by the United States army when they were putting through the Alaska highway and the Canol pipe line. It is a veritable fire trap and it is inefficient; but it does the job. The plans had reached the point where there are working drawings for the new hospital. This project is now at a halt. I do not know how many times since last April I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether a decision had been reached with respect to the Charles Camsell hospital. I always received the usual answer, "No decision has yet been reached. When one is arrived at, you will be advised". I must confess, Mr. Chairman, that I think I would have received a little better action under other circumstances. It is high time the government made up its mind one way or the other with respect to this hospital. If the government decides to follow the recommendation of the Glassco commission report, I would say to the minister this would be a most retrograde step with respect to the health services for our Indians and Eskimos.
It is true that there is a hospital at Inuvik and there is a hospital at Whitehorse. But for the long term treatment of tuberculosis and some of the other diseases which are more difficult to eradicate there is nothing

like the Charles Camsell hospital in Edmonton, where you have the most highly qualified medical practitioners available as consultants, where there is a good staff within the Department of National Health and Welfare, people who are dedicated to their work. I will simply tell the committee that last January I went through the hospital on the occasion of the awarding of scholarship certificates. These were awarded to a young Eskimo from Inuvik who was going into second year medicine, a girl who was going into education but who was a patient at the hospital-these were university students-and a girl who had just received her certificate from a commercial school and was going out to work as a stenographer. Every year I have had the opportunity of congratulating these young people who have made their mark, who have achieved something. They are examples to other young people among the Indian and Eskimo populations.
Just a few months prior to that the hospital had been closed at Hobbema, which is located in the constituency of my colleague the hon. member for Wetaskiwin. It was indicated to the Indians on the two reserves at Hobbema that they could go into the Wetaskiwin or the Ponoka county hospitals. What was the result? The registrations in the Camsell hospital during January and February, 1962, were up by 45 each month in respect of people from those two reserves. You ask the Indians, "Why do you come here to Edmonton when you could be so much closer to your homes at Wetaskiwin or Ponoka?" They say, "We come among people who know us, who understand us. We are here with patients from other reserves. We have rehabilitation services here. We are welcomed in this hospital". We know that in the county, municipal and city hospitals the overcrowding is fantastic. Unless you are just about dying and require an emergency operation you cannot get into some hospitals. If they are queuing up from the white population to go into our very limited general hospitals, how is it to be expected that our Indians and Eskimos will be accepted? If an Indian woman wants to come into hospital to have a child, is she going to go into a general maternity ward? Today she will not. A generation from now, she may. So I would urge the minister to give this matter serious consideration.
I do not want to belabour the point but I wish to re-emphasize everything I have said in correspondence with his office and the office of his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Charles Camsell hospital must be rebuilt. Ultimately it may be made into a general hospital, but that is a generation from now. I think this would be one step in helping these people to integrate.

We should not give them the sort of cold water treatment of saying, "All right; we are taking your hospital away from you. You can now fend for yourselves in the local hospitals". That is not good enough and it would be a retrograde step.
Still on the subject of Indians and Eskimos, Mr. Chairman, there is a residential school in my riding to which some young Indians are brought from northern British Columbia to attend the city schools.
On examining the situation as to the training for the Indians at Yellowknife and some of the other training schools, I think that somehow we have missed the boat. We take these Indians from their homes while they are still in their early teens, and perhaps younger, put them in a white man's school, teach them white man's training and white man's habits, and then at the age of 16 turn them back to the reserves or among their own families. They are not adapted to Indian native habits. They have not acquired skills in hunting. They have the white man's skills, but no agency is there to follow up and see that they use that training.
The minister may say, "Well, we do for a bit." But is it not like a child learning to walk. You are asking these young people to go from a crawl to a walk and, Mr. Chairman, you know that a child learning to walk will stumble many times. You have to pick him up and get him back on his feet. I suggest that a massive assault must be made on this problem. It may take a generation. I hope it will take less, but these young Indians have got to be followed up, and this must be a government policy decision.
I hoped I was convincing the minister's predecessor in this regard to start such a program, but it does not concern only the minister within his department. He must convince his colleagues that there has to be a massive assault on this whole problem. It may take 10, 15 or 20 years, but if we do not do it we will not have a satisfactory solution that will help these people become self-reliant, more adapted to modern ways, and able to form an integral part of our population. If we can do that, we will have achieved something and the increased moneys we will have to spend will be worth while.
There are several reservations in and around the Edmonton area. They are handled through what is called the Edmonton agency, where there is an officer in charge, with various Indian agents operating out of the Edmonton office. I wonder whether this is right. It has been put to me by people who know Indians, and have been associated with them for many years, that it might be better if the Indian agent as a general rule lived on a reservation. There may be a paternal
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration aspect to this, but there is a benefit in his being there and knowing the people. He is not then an office man who comes out to them three times a week.
I shall now switch to the subject of immigration. I have discussed privately with the minister something which I hope he will look into, the acceptance as immigrants to this country of more young people from the other side of the iron curtain. There should be an extension of the rules regarding relationship, so that we can admit young people under the age of 21 for the purpose of reuniting members of families, where the senior members of families in Canada are well established, in the position to take in further relatives, and are willing to do so.
Some excuses have been made on the basis of security, and one thing or another, but I will put this question: Is the government's policy more concerned with immigration or security? By this I do not mean any disrespect to the R.C.M.P. who have a difficult problem to deal with. As I say, I have discussed this with the minister privately, particularly with reference to countries like Poland and Czechoslovakia, provided of course the governments of those countries will release their nationals to come to Canada. We cannot drag people here from those countries.
Gracious me, are boys and girls of 15 or 16 years such subversives that they cannot be admitted to this country on the same basis as orphaned nephews or nieces? What is wrong with extending the regulation to cover second cousins? We are prepared to make exceptions for nephews, nieces and unmarried children, so what great danger would there be in extending the regulation to cover grand nephews, grand nieces and second cousins? We would be doing a great service in uniting members of families and assisting them to become economic units. If there is a step that can be taken in the right direction with regard to immigration, it is in this area, and I suggest it apply to countries on the other side of the iron curtain, and indeed to all the countries of Europe.
This afternoon the hon. member for Lot-biniere spoke about the disparity in the figures of immigration from France and from the Anglo-Saxon countries.

He referred to the Belgians and the French. When you mention the Belgians, you have to speak of the Walloons and the Flemish.
As for me, I am of Flemish origin, and I know there is quite a difference. I know also that my grandparents never thought of themselves as French speaking, despite the fact that they could speak the language.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
And I can tell the minister it is quite likely that, out of the thousands of French immigrants that we have received within the last two generations, many have left the country. As a matter of fact, before I was elected to this house and at the request of the American consul, I used to translate and check the documents of the French and Belgian people who wished to obtain a certificate executed and authenticated by a notary.
I then translated law reports, military bulletins, etc., and I can tell the minister that, from the outset, namely some time before 1954 or 1955,1 cannot remember a single week when I was not required to translate such documents for French people who had immigrated to Canada and were going to the United States. When they were asked why they were doing so, they answered: Well, here, in Canada, the weather is very cold. Most of these immigrants were coming, so it seems, from southern France, and they were going to California. We could not keep them here and this is the reason for this lack of balance in the field of immigration.

There is one further brief point I would like to make with the minister, and it concerns Chinese immigration. Those of us who represent western cities have more contact with the problem of Chinese immigration than our colleagues from eastern Canada. I have heard, not only from the minister but from his predecessor, about the staff difficulties in Hong Kong, and I would like to know what has been done to ameliorate those difficulties in the last year? I still get from time to time queries about applications for immigration, where a potential immigrant has been told to come back for an interview in four or five months. This does not do much good, when a wife with small children is told to come back in four or five months.
This situation has existed for some time. Is it to be tolerated forever? I suggest to the minister that so far as Chinese immigrants are concerned we in western cities would welcome a lot more. They represent in the city of Edmonton I suppose one half of 1 per cent of the population, if that. They are not what used to be the popular conception of a Chinese citizen. Many of them are professional gentlemen, excellent businessmen. Second, the second generation Chinese are of the very best citizens within our communities. I think that here we can do something. I would ask the minister to let the house know what has been done to straighten out the situation in Hong Kong. I know there is a great deal of pressure in this quarter, but it seems to me that there has not been a great

increase in staff to handle it. We still get some of the same complaints about officials. I would say that almost one out of three applications by Chinese immigrants results in recourse being had to a member of parliament to see whether the application could be pushed and set moving. Strangely enough, when you do get behind it, it does move. So what is happening? Is it because more pressure is required? If so, all right, we will put on the pressure. But I think the minister recognizes the problem, so I would ask him to take the committee into his confidence and to tell us what he has done and what he anticipates doing in regard to this problem.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak very briefly indeed. I do so because I have received a letter from the minister's special assistant regarding a case which I mentioned when I last spoke on the estimates. I rise to deal briefly with the circumstances and to ask the minister a question, to which I trust I will receive a favourable reply, this being Christmas time.
I refer the minister to the application of Mr. Wong Hong Taw for the admission to Canada of his son Wong Yun Lam from Hong Kong. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister at the request of numerous people in Kootenay West who have known the old gentleman for many years. He is a splendid old chap. His application was supported by a petition of some 50 names, including one official of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, the mayor of Trail, prominent business people and other persons. It is rather a pathetic case. I was under the impression that Mr. Wong Hong Taw had more assets than appears to be the case at the moment. He was at one time quite a prosperous market gardener, but recently he has suffered from ill health. The minister was kind enough to have this case reviewed and referred to his official in Nelson, who has reported to the minister. I just want to refer to the letter and then ask the minister a question. The letter is dated December 16 last, addressed to me, and it reads as follows: Dear Mr. Herridge:
I refer to my letter of November 29, 1963, concerning the application of Mr. Wong Hong Taw for the admission to Canada of his son, Wong Yun Lam, from Hong Kong.
The immigration officials have had a report from their officer in Nelson, B.C. who states that Wong Hong Taw is almost destitute, having no assets either in cash or real estate, and being a recipient of somewhat meagre welfare payments. Under the circumstances, the applicant cannot meet minimal requirements for settlement arrangements for his son.
Mr. F. C. Crosman's letter of July 11, 1963, commented on Wong Yun Lam's limited qualifications. The report of the Hong Kong immigration officials.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
on which Mr. Crosman's letter was based, clearly indicated that Wong Yun Lam could not qualify as an unsponsored immigrant.
The previous decision in this case can therefore only be sustained. In view of your interest, I regret that my reply is not more favourable.
I am returning herewith the documents which you left with me in connection with this application.
Yours sincerely,
Peter Bosa,
Special Assistant.
So, Mr. Chairman, I am rising again at the request of a number of people in my constituency who are very concerned about the welfare of this really lovable old man whom they have known for many years. I understand the circumstances and the reason for the minister's reply, but I ask him this question. If the hon. member for Kootenay West sponsors this young man and guarantees that he will never be a public charge, will he be admitted to Canada to stay with his father?
