speechtext: Shall the item carry?

Only one question, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I have only two questions to ask. I should like to ask the minister whether his department intends to implement the report of the Glassco commission, which suggests to allot the issuing of passports to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration rather than to the Department of External Affairs.
My second question is this. Did the minister, who is very close to the government of the province of Quebec, meet the authorities of that government to suggest that the province of Quebec should make the necessary efforts to be in a position of extending a better welcome to the immigrants, as the other provinces do, especially Ontario?
In this connection, I am inspired by an article published in Le Devoir on November 10, 1963 and which reported the statement made by Mr. Lesage on television:
The province of Quebec should take the necessary means so that immigrants be given a better welcome on their arrival in Quebec province.
Those are the only comments I had to make on this question.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to take a few minutes of the committee's time to express my approval of the statement made this afternoon by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) concerning the immigration to Canada of French speaking people.
I know that I can develop the hon. member's arguments because, unfortunately, he
was unable to do so himself since the party whip likes nothing better than to restrain the members of his group.
I regret to inform the member that it is not so.

As for me, I feel much freer on this side of the house, I can express any opinion I hold.
Mr. Chairman, I agree with the statements made this afternoon by the hon. member for Lotbiniere. Of course, as in all the speeches he has been making these last three or four days, he began by praising a good deal the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. However, I agree that in that case the praise was well deserved. In fact, I wish to take the opportunity to say that the minister has a brilliant future in his party.
However, Mr. Chairman, a fact remains. According to the figures quoted this afternoon there is a disproportion between immigration from English speaking countries and immigration from French speaking countries and there are many reasons for that. What solutions could be brought to the problem?
I believe that the first one would be a better concerted and better prepared publicity in the French speaking countries.
I also believe that the minister should give more attention to another important fact which is the supervision of the emigration of a great number of Canadian citizens to the United States. If we take into account the number of citizens of the province of Quebec and other provinces who have, since the beginning of this century, left Canada to go and work in other countries, we will find that this emigration has been harmful and even disastrous for us. One of its causes can be found in the facts of life.
For instance, the lumberman in the Belle-chasse, Beauce, Dorchester, Kamouraska and Temiscouata constituencies, and so forth, go to work in the United States in winter, and when they come back into the country, they do not benefit from the assistance their country gives in the field of unemployment insurance. Well, when that happens, these Canadian citizens are inclined to try to emigrate to the United States, where they may take advantage of the social legislation in that country.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration might perhaps urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to have our Canadian citizens share in all the social benefits to which they are entitled.
Mr. Chairman, I have a last comment to make. For some time, a debate has gone on between the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in Ottawa and the minister of national resources in Quebec in order to find

6250	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration who will have charge of the administration- and at the same time, who will have jurisdiction over the educational system-of the Eskimos and Indians living in New Quebec or in the north of the province.
I submit it is quite an important problem to consider. Perhaps, at the present time, a rather limited number of individuals are involved, but there is every reason to believe that, within a relatively short period, mining or industrial developments will take place in that part of the province of Quebec. At that time, Eskimos and white men will live side by side, and one of the two groups will come under the authority of the provincial administration, whereas the other will live under federal jurisdiction. Then, that problem will be more acute than it is now. That is why I think the minister should give it his whole attention in order to anticipate the related problems which will come up within ten or 12 years in that area. Problems will inevitably come up if the present situation keeps up, when New Quebec and the far north are developed. But if we anticipate the problems -I think that what is wrong with the government at the present time is that corrective measures are taken only when the problems come up-if, in that area, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, with the capability we know he has, could anticipate the difficulties and find the solution right away, then, we would avoid for the future generations, discussions which might be very bitter.
Mr. Chairman, those are the three points I wanted to submit to the minister, and I would sum them up like this: French immigration in our country; disastrous emigration of too many Canadian citizens to the United States; and the Eskimos and Indians living in northern Quebec.
I hope the minister will take those problems into consideration and that in his next estimates, he will be in a position to tell us what he intends to do to settle them.

Mr. Chairman, I shall start by replying right away to the three questions that have been asked. First of all, I shall answer the question dealing with the recommendations of the Glassco commission concerning passports. This recommendation will be looked into. I must say, however, that the matter does not come under my depart-mnt as such, but concerns rather the study group which is presently considering the recommendations of the Glassco commission. In any case, that is one of the points under consideration at present.
Second, with regard to the discussions with the Quebec government, I must say that the discussions held were informal [Mr. Gregoire.l
rather than official. I have already had or started to have talks. I feel confident that, in the future, my views in that regard will prevail.

As to the matter raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West, I am not in a position, in full committee, to settle a specific question of this kind; but I can tell the hon. member that in view of the sympathetic nature of the proponent of the question I cannot help but consider the matter very sympathetically.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I first wish to thank the hon. members who made such flattering remarks about me. I simply consider them as an encouragement to perform my duty in the future as I have done up to now.
Some constructive suggestions have been made, several have already been implemented and others are under consideration. We must not forget that criticism is still one of the best ways to expedite public business. I thank the members for their constructive criticisms.
I would like to say a word about Chinese immigration. I hope that I did not convey the impression, in my remarks, that Chinese immigration, which evidently involved some complex problems, had been overlooked by the department.
May I say on the matter of sponsorship that there will be a broadening of the plan with respect to families, particularly in the speeding up of consideration and disposal of requests which are being processed.
Many protracted meetings have already taken place in that connection with my officials, and I can even promise the committee that within the next year, recommendations will be submitted to the cabinet and, for this reason, I am not free to disclose, for the time being, the solutions I intend to propose.
Now I must point out that in 1961, 661 immigrants of Chinese origin were admitted into Canada, that 826 came into this country in 1962 and that, during the first nine months of 1963, 1,008 have already been admitted, which means that this year we will substantially exceed the number of immigrants of Chinese origin admitted up to now.
Two weeks ago, the acting director of the immigration branch went to Hong Kong at my request, and I intend to follow him soon. As a result of recommendations, we have already applied measures which will reduce by 50 per cent the work and time involved in the processing of applications of Hong Kong immigrants.

In the course of their remarks, some members have asked whether or not Anal consideration has been given by me to the case of Miss Irene Rebrin who immigrated to Canada in 1958 and who was ordered deported in January, 1959. I must say that this case was relatively complex. It involved certain delicate factors and it was my intention to give it all the consideration required. I am pleased to inform the committee that the review of this case has now been completed. I have decided that Miss Rebrin should now be admitted to Canada as a landed immigrant. The necessary procedures are being commenced to adjust her status. The conclusion I have reached takes into account the current circumstances and it is not intended to have any bearing on the past treatment of this case or to imply that any decision made in the past in this respect was improper at the time it was made.
I have stated, Mr. Chairman, that it is at least my opinion, because we are dealing with human beings directly, that in these cases the minister should refrain-I do not say that in the past the minister has not refrained-from any comparison between his own policies and the policies of previous ministers or governments. This is why I wish to make it very clear that the Rebrin case has been looked into in the light of the facts as they existed in December of 1963. If an immigrant is refused in 1959, for instance, under section 5 because this immigrant suffers from a disease, and if the matter is looked at in 1963 and that person has been cured, a decision is then made in the light of the factors as they exist in 1963 and may not be interpreted as reflecting unfavourably on any previous decision.
I am not unmindful also in taking this decision, and I think it is important, that there is presently pending a libel suit between Miss Rebrin and somebody else. As a lawyer I have considered that and I know I am satisfied in my own mind that in the suit the facts, of course, will be looked at as they were in 1959, and not 1963, and that consequently any decision I may make may not be used for or against anybody in the case, because anything which I might say would not be acceptable legal evidence. It would be purely hearsay. So I thought it was my duty to make the decision, and having arrived at that conclusion, I am pleased to state it to the house tonight.
May I say just one word with respect to Indian affairs. In a jocular fashion but in a way seriously, I know, it has been suggested that the minister try to devise a system whereby he will ensure that the important
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration branch of his department known as Indian affairs will disappear in 20 years. I must say I cannot agree more. I also know that when I say this my officials will not be frightened by the proposition because, knowing their dedication to their cause, I know that they all agree. This is the objective and the purpose, that once the Indians have fully succeeded in adjusting themselves to our present way of life in a fashion compatible with their own traditions and original culture and also in the freest possible way there will not then be any necessity for an Indian affairs branch as such. This objective, of course, embodies a requirement for the implementation of all of those measures which we have discussed during the presentation and discussion of these estimates.
May I say a last word on matters of immigration about the relaxation of what have been called the rules of relationship. This is one of the subjects which, as many members know, I have most deeply at heart at present. Rules which were probably necessary at the time they were made have caused difficulty, and ways and means must be found to adapt them to more humane conditions of immigration.
My last word is to join with hon. members in congratulating the new deputy minister of my department on his accession to that high position. I must say that if the first 30 days of his presence in the department are a sign of the future, and I know they are, there will be a great future for the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister on his decision with reference to the Rebrin case and say to him that many of us are highly pleased at the excellent beginning he has made in the handling of his department. We look forward to a very enlightened period of administration under his guidance.
I should like to ask him one brief question. I have reference now to the Mrs. Miriam Stevenson case which I raised in the house on the orders of the day some weeks ago and about which I wrote the minister. I do not want to take much time of the committee but I would like the minister to give, if he can, some assurance with reference to the immediate status of this case. I do not know Mrs. Stevenson nor am I familiar with all the details of her case. I do know that, according to press reports, she is a citizen of Great Britain, that she lived for a while in the United States and that she is now being deported because in the 1930's she was for one year, it is claimed, a member of the communist party. She contends that she has had no association whatsoever with the communist party since the 1930's.
6252	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
The minister was gracious enough to grant a stay of proceedings for 60 days on this case during which time she and her legal counsel are requested to produce evidence to prove that she has dissociated herself from her former connections. I hope she can do that but, as I pointed out to the minister when I wrote him, it is very difficult to prove a negative. How you prove that you no longer are something is extremely difficult. She may be able to get character references or people who will express opinions, but I do not know how you can prove you are not something. It may be possible to prove that you are a member of an organization, but how you prove you are not a member of an organization seems to me extremely difficult.
It may not be possible within the time limit she has to produce this kind of evidence. Therefore I want to ask the minister first of all whether it will be possible, if that evidence is not forthcoming and it appears to him that the case is deserving of consideration, to extend the time during which she can endeavour to get this kind of evidence. Second, is it the intention of the minister to review the act to see if some of these very wide discretionary powers which are given to the minister could be spelled out in the act? It seems to me that the powers are very wide when the whole discretion whether or not this woman, who is a British subject, who has lived in Canada and who is now in her late 50's, will be deported lies entirely with the minister. It so happens I am fairly well satisfied with the discretion of this minister, but that is not the point at issue. The point is whether or not this is a discretion which is far too great to reside in any one person, without any right of appeal.

I have just a brief word or two before the item passes. The minister made a statement a while ago which will be pleasant sounding music to the ears of native Indian people of Canada, namely that it is his desire that within 20 years or a reasonable period of time there will no longer be a need for an Indian affairs branch, or the Indian Act for that matter. It has been one of the sore points in the minds of the native Indian people for many years, that they should be singled out and subjected to a law and an administration specifically dealing with them on a racial or ethnic basis. As I said earlier in my remarks, and I hope the minister will not take this personally because it is not intended that way, the Indian people feel that there is a need for action rather than words. Words have been directed to them time after time in years gone by. It is action that will impress them at this point.


I have great hopes that what the minister says will be accomplished will, in fact, be accomplished.
I have a question or two I should like to direct to the minister about a problem I raised earlier. However, it might be as well to wait until the item is called which deals with welfare.

As the member who first raised the case of Irene Rebrin in the house I wish to thank the department on behalf of the people in British Columbia. I am sure the minister has made a lot of people in British Columbia happy to hear that he considered the unfortunate plight of this young lady.

I should like to ask a question of the minister with reference to the order in council concerning Weldon Chan. This is a man who broke every law in Canada and who went underground for three years. Suddenly, he is pardoned by order in council. Now, how do I advise my constituents, a lot of whom come from eastern Europe? Do I tell them to bring their relatives in, admit nothing and hope that they will be pardoned by the minister? This was the most disgraceful thing that ever happened in this country.

Is the minister going to say anything about the matter I raised earlier concerning the opening up of old orders in council to try to ascertain where the difficulties lie in the cases that have come before the department?

I am sorry if I forgot that question. I first wish to thank the hon. gentleman for having agreed to my suggestion to restrict the area of his very broad question. Vote No. 60 covers the operation of the welfare branch of Indian affairs, with which I dealt in an earlier part of my remarks. There is an agreement, I have not got it with me now, but I believe it is headed, statement of policy on health or welfare services, and it is an agreement between the government of Canada and the province of British Columbia. Perhaps there are similar agreements with other provinces, I do not know. The effect of this agreement which came into force this past January, as I read it, is that if an Indian lives on a reserve and is eligible to receive welfare, he will receive that assistance at the rate established by the Indian affairs branch, namely $22 per month. Then, if there are any dependants the amount decreases to $15 per month for dependants over 12 years of age and $12 per month for dependants under 12. I do not know if these figures are correct. However, if an Indian person lives off the reserve for a period of time and is eligible for welfare assistance, he receives welfare assistance at the rate paid by the provincial department, which is substantially in excess of the amount paid by the Indian affairs branch.
Then, if a non-Indian living on the reserve is eligible for or in need of welfare assistance, he will receive that assistance at the rate payable by the Indian affairs branch. If he is living off the reserve, of course, the agreement does not apply. The essence of this agreement is that it sets up two schedules of welfare payments for Indian people, one when they are on the reserve and one when they are off the reserve. In view of the desire of governments-as enunciated also by the minister recently-within the last couple of years that the goal and objective should be what we loosely call the transfer of jurisdiction over these matters to the provincial government, I wonder whether the minister could tell us what plans are afoot to either discard that agreement or revise it in such a way that there is equality of welfare payments to native Indian people as compared with people of non-Indian origin. I am talking about British Columbia, but I am sure that if similar agreements are in existence in other provinces and the same sort of discriminatory system prevails, naturally what I have said applies to those provinces also.

Mr. Chairman, first I must say that it is probably a laudable objective to even out as much as possible the rates of welfare payments. But surely no member of an Indian community may complain about the fact that when they go off the reserve and live somewhere else in the province the

I do not want to justify the rate that is paid to Indians, and I do not say it is not justifiable either. I must say that the rate paid to Indians on the reserve is for food only, but Indians living off the reserve have considerable additional expenses which those on the reserve do not have, including provision for lodging, heating, fuel and other factors. Indians living off the reserve have to meet these expenses and those on the reserve do not have to meet them.
In the same way it is true that the rates vary even from province to province, and so long as uniformity between the provinces is not achieved, even if we adjusted the rates as applied to Indians there would, because of the different levels in the provinces, remain certain differences. It is our objective to level out these things as much as possible. I think we will be in a position to do a great deal with respect to looking into this question in depth at the conference which takes place in the month of May between the federal minister and the appropriate provincial ministers. As I said, this conference is in preparation and the agenda will soon be discussed among the provinces and the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, I anticipated that the conference which arose out of the recently concluded dominion-provincial conference would provide the arena for the discussion of a great many of these matters. I only wanted to raise the question with the minister now, so that it is on the record once again and we do not lose track of it in the wealth of all the other things that take place; because this is an important matter. The minister said-and I am paraphrasing him now-that surely no Indian living off the reserve would complain that he is receiving the welfare assistance payable by the province. Perhaps they do not, but an Indian person does complain in this way. They look at the disparity in welfare payments as a result of this agreement and say, "Ah, ah; here is another attempt by the government to entice us to get off the reserve. They are now using the enticement of increased welfare payments to do it". I say this because, as the minister well knows, the history of the treatment of native Indian people by law has been full of enticements for them to become enfranchised, to leave the reserve, to lose their status as an Indian. These enticements involve the right to vote, which was granted a few years ago. They involved liquor, and still do to a certain


extent. They involve the amount of band funds the Indian gets when he becomes enfranchised, and so on.
Most of the Indian people have resented the fact that enticements have been offered to get them to cease being Indians within the meaning of the Indian Act. They want to retain their history, culture and association with their own people. They look upon this agreement, with its disparity in the approach to welfare, as being another enticement by government to get them off the reserve. It is unfortunate that this attitude exists. I can only hope at this moment that when the federal-provincial conference on Indian affairs is held it will do something to correct this discrimination. Everyone will be praying for it to come up with something that is reasonable, decent and conclusive with respect to Indian affairs, so we can take the step the Indian has been looking for, for so long-* the step toward equality and decency of treatment for them.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to remind the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau) of my request addressed to him last November in favour of Indians belonging to the La Manouane reserve who are deprived at the present time of all medical assistance. I have been in recent contact with officers of the minister and I pointed out to them that I had been told by the reserve chief that it would be advantageous for a doctor to practise in that reserve. As I am aware of the minister's concern with problems relating to his department, I feel sure that the Indians of La Manouane will be given, in the future, the medical assistance that is essential to that community.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I am quite prepared to move very rapidly on these items if the minister will give us a short statement on the NATO conference, and any developments at that conference, and bring us up to date on the recent changes that we read about in the newspapers concerning national defence. We would like to hear about these matters right here in the house.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the NATO conference I would be pleased to make a very brief report. It was, in my opinion, a most satisfactory conference. There had been some apprehension, I believe, that certain issues would be divisive, or could possibly be divisive; but there was no evidence of this at the conference. There was reaffirmation of the solidarity of the 15 nations which compose the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We received a first class briefing of the military threat which presently exists from the Soviet union, an assessment of their strengths and of their capabilities. If anything, the consensus was that the conventional strength of the Soviet union, when given a qualitative analysis, is not as great as was previously estimated, but of course is still quite formidable.
We also heard a very interesting statement in respect to the western capabilities, the forces available to meet the threat, and the state of the alliance from the military standpoint at the present time.
On behalf of the Canadian delegation we had a statement which made the council aware of the defence review which is presently being undertaken here, and which mentioned certain decisions that already have been taken and of which the council were already aware. It also indicated that one or two other matters were under consultation at present with the military authorities, and that these would be presented to the permanent council in the usual way as soon as agreement was reached.
It was pointed out that our review in this country was really in two phases. The first phase dealt largely with procurement, which is now completed. We attempted not to procure equipment which would limit the options
Supply-National Defence open to us in future years. The second phase of our review was in respect to longer term policy, and that in determining longer term policy the government would be very much aware of the relationship between our armed forces, and those of our allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. This statement seemed to be well received, as were any consultations we had with military and civilian authorities at the conference.
I think the most notable achievement of the whole meeting was the reaffirmation of solidarity, and the undertaking on the part of all members of the alliance not to stand in the way of going ahead and working out problems which arise from time to time, as is inevitable in any alliance of 15 nations in peacetime. In summary, it was a most satisfactory conference and we in the Canadian delegation took satisfaction from it.
With respect to the hon. gentleman's second question, it is unfortunate that consultations are not yet complete and therefore I am reluctant to say anything more at this time. It is not helpful to give information in detail before negotiations have been worked out, and these negotiations are presently under way. The NATO military authorities have been advised of any proposals the government of Canada has at the present time. These are being studied, staff work is being done at the moment, and we expect to hear back in the not too distant future. I would hope it will be possible within a few weeks to make public any additional information that is relevant to the slight adjustments which have been proposed.

Could the minister give us some information regarding two matters recently reported in the press. One is a report which appeared in the Globe and Mail of December 20 and which says:
The Royal Canadian Air Force base at Gros-tenquin, France, will be closed, a highly placed source said yesterday.
The other Canadian base in France, at Marville, will be retained but the CF-104 nuclear bombers there will be converted to a strictly conventional, reconnaissance role, the source said-
The CF-104's at Grostenquin will be moved to the German bases.
Is this the plan which the department has in mind? Is it intended to close the first base and move the aircraft to Germany, and is it also the intention to keep the Marville base open but to change the equipment on the CF-104's so that they can be used for conventional purposes?
The other matter is with reference to an announcement which came from Paris while the minister was there. There were some conflicting reports about this. I gather some of the papers were quoting the statement as though it came from the minister, but later

Supply-National Defence I received a more accurate report which said it came from British military sources. It was a statement to the effect that an agreement had been signed permitting the British V-bomber force to be trained in Canada and it said-
-that the R.A.F.'s nuclear V-bomber force is to use Canadian air space to test a new "low-level" attack strategy.
It also said:
-the V-bombers would operate from Canadian bases, covering "distances in northern Canada similar to those which would be met in a retaliatory assault on Russia."
Most people felt this was hardly the way to contribute to a lessening of international tensions, and to strengthen the detente which it is hoped we are building between the east and the west since the signing of the partial nuclear test ban agreement.
I would like the minister to give some explanation why this new training program is being launched? Is a new agreement being entered into, or is it being done under some former agreement? Will it mean a great increase in the British personnel located in Canada, or is it simply an old program being blown up for publicity purposes by the British government, which is sorely in need of being bolstered on the home front?

The Globe and Mail report is one of a series which has appeared in respect to the proposed adjustments to the air division. It is not too inaccurate in respect to a proposal that has been made by the Canadian government, and is a pretty fair reflection, though not quite complete, of the suggestions we have made to the military authorities in NATO. I would prefer if the hon. member allow me not to go beyond that in spelling it out, because I feel we have some obligation to our allies not to pre-publicize in detail suggestions which have been put forward while they are in fact subject to consultation.
I believe the second report had an unfortunate emphasis. It is true, and this much I confirmed while in Paris, that there has been agreement to permit British V-bombers to use a low-level training route in Canada. This is not really a new situation because we have made air space available to the British for training purposes many times, and it is really just an extension of the long standing cooperation existing between the Canadian government and the R.A.F. This involves a technique of contour flying, low level flying which requires special training.
The difficulty is in obtaining routes which do not unduly interfere with the civilian population. Particularly in England such routes are just not available. For that reason

a request came forward to make available a route in Canada which would be over part of our territory, but which would not be an undue nuisance to the civilian population. A route was selected and permission given to operate this one route. It does not mean that there will be any sizeable augmentation of British personnel in Canada. It will just be a staging operation. Planes will come over. I think they are to operate from Goose Bay; they will fly this training route perhaps on several successive days, and then fly back to their regular bases in the United Kingdom.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the minister for his concise reply. I only want to say one thing, that when he tells us about reports in the Globe and Mail referring to the disposition of the CF-104's, the closing of one base in France and the retention of the other for the use of CF-104's which are being converted to a conventional role, it makes me somewhat apprehensive of the fact that this is about the third or fourth time in recent months that highly informed sources have been able with amazing accuracy to prophesy what the minister is going to announce. Again I imagine that somebody has stolen the minister's thunder and has told the public what the minister has only now told the House of Commons. I can understand the reluctance of the minister not to tell the House of Commons until the matter has been cleared up with our allies, but I should point out to the minister that it is a little disconcerting for parliament to find that most of the policies of the Department of National Defence seem to be announced in the press a week or two before they are announced in the house. While there might be a certain amount of guesswork going on, the accuracy with which these prophecies have been fulfilled makes one think that the minister ought to look and see whether there is a leak somewhere in his information set-up, or whether the minister himself is deliberately flying a kite-I do not know which it is.

May I say that the minister is a little apprehensive too. This information did not come from my office, if that is what the hon. gentleman is suggesting. Up to this moment I have not been able to find out just who the informed source was. I should like to know the answer to that question, and if the hon. member can assist me I would be most grateful. I find it a little disconcerting myself, because at noon I was eating in the restaurant and one of my colleagues, a member of parliament, introduced me to a young officer, who informed me to my face in front of my friend exactly what we proposed to do. So that when we refer to informed sources, it

seems to me there are quite a few of them, and it is very difficult to tell exactly which one it is.
For this reason I try to make the information public as quickly as possible. That was certainly one of the main reasons for making so many announcements on the estimates, even though they actually applied to next year's estimates, so as to end the rumours and speculation and to get the information on the record. I would be pleased to put the information respecting the other readjustments on the record just as fast as can be arranged in order to end this type of speculation, which I find a little interesting, as does my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that the estimates of the department now before us are the most important of all the federal budget. As a matter of fact, the Minister of National Defence surely is the most greedy of all, since he takes for his department alone more than 25 per cent of the money collected from Canadian taxpayers.
I would now like to make the following remarks. I am amazed, like many other Canadians, to see that in a period such as this, the Department of National Defence has found it advisable to have three submarines built in England for the Canadian navy, while so many Canadian workers in our shipyards are now unemployed and greatly need the work that would have been provided by the construction, in Canada, of those three submarines.
I submit that the Minister of National Defence, before making other commitments of this kind and before granting to other countries contracts to build submarines, or aircraft, or any other type of military hardware, should first endeavour to grant them to Canadian industries, factories or shipyards.
If the Minister of National Defence could meet the Canadian people, he would realize that the public is voicing strong protests against his department's decision to award those contracts to foreigners while there is unemployment in Canada.
There are two or three other questions I should like to ask the minister.
First, are any nuclear arms stored at present at Bagotville for the Voodoos which are stationed there?
Second, if there are no nuclear weapons there now, when is it expected that a stockpile will be established?
Third, will the Voodoos stationed in Bagotville make daily flights or will they be allowed to carry nuclear weapons during their daily or regular flights?

I know the minister did not make the decision, but can he give the committee any information as to the basis on which Canada purchased a type of CF-104 for our R.C.A.F. squadrons in Europe capable only of using nuclear weapons, whereas all the F-104's used by other countries were built with a dual purpose possibility. Why was Canada the only country which bought an aircraft with a strictly nuclear capacity? The CF-104 must have been built that way


with the knowledge of the previous government. They must have known it could never be used, except with nuclear warheads.

First of all I might answer the hon. member for Lapointe. He asked if there are nuclear weapons now at Bagotville. The answer is, no. He asked when there will be nuclear weapons there. I do not know; probably late next year. He asked whether there will be daily flights with nuclear weapons aboard aircraft. The answer is, no. He asked what the danger would be to the people in the area when these weapons are adopted. May I say that every possible precaution is taken. We have safety procedures which are as good as can be devised and the success of these measures is shown by the fact that throughout all these years the United States has had nuclear warheads numbering many thousands, there has never been an accidental nuclear explosion. Every conceivable precaution is taken.
I am not familiar with all the reasoning which went into the particular configuration of the CF-104. It was part of the development of a new weapons platform embarked upon by a number of nations in co-operation. Canada shared the cost of that development. Our particular configuration was a little different from the F-104G which is used by some of our allies, but it does have some built-in capabilities. This would make it possible to adopt a dual role for part of the air division if that should prove to be the proper solution. The aircraft is capable of carrying bombs of various kinds. A Gatling gun can be installed. It is possible to fire rockets if the pods and the rockets are purchased. There are a number of minor modifications which, if undertaken, would give the plane non-nuclear capacity. The cost would vary according to what was done, but it would not be great. The necessary wiring is all built into the aircraft, and though some minor modifications would be necessary the cost would not be great in proportion to the total amount of money involved in the program.

Perhaps the minister did not follow my question. The F-104, with which a number of other countries are equipped is constructed with a dual capacity. Only the CF-104, which we have has been so constructed that it is only capable of delivering nuclear warheads. I believe this is a fact. If it is, can the minister explain why?

As I was saying, although the CF-104 was designed specifically for the strike role, it does have this capability of being easily adapted to a number of roles without need for major modification. The

capacity is built in so as to give considerable flexibility. It really is not very different from the F-104G.

I acquired in the army a technique of work and things that I could not acquire in universities because they had not been put at my disposal. Mr. Chairman, I object to two allegations made by the member for Beauharnois-Salaberry. He said he had received in the army things that he could not get at the university. Mr. Chairman, I could not let pass without protesting that insult to our universities, because I think the universities of the province of Quebec can give-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It seems that the discussion just started between two hon. members is not of a nature to advance the business of the committee and I would ask them to forget strictly educational matters to come back to item No. 1 now before us.

Mr. Chairman, I am willing to co-operate in order to accelerate progress of the business of the house, but not at the expense of the honour and reputation of the universities of the province of Quebec which are equal to the task-
Learn to have some self-discipline.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) is insulting the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) by attributing to him words he has never uttered. And I think that before lecturing anybody in this house, the hon. member for Lapointe should have the honesty to report faithfully the statements that were made.

Mr. Chairman, tomorrow's Hansard will report the words said tonight by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry when he stated that he received in the army a training which he could not get at the university.
And I believe that tomorrow's Hansard will amply prove that the member really made the statement I pointed out.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The only thing I wish to have recorded in Hansard is that I want the hon. member for Lapointe to know I never had the opportunity to attend university. If he had listened, he would have understood what I said, that is I did not acquire at the university what I was able to acquire in the army, since my basic schooling did not permit me to attend university. But, the army has nevertheless enabled me to be elected to this house and to serve my country perhaps even better than the member for Lapointe.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to note the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry at last succeeded in explaining

what he wanted to say. I agree it was complicated enough, but by keeping on trying, he finally succeeded.
However, I maintain my statement to the effect that education comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces and not the army, and that the suggestion to make military service compulsory is contrary to the democratic principles we all cherish in this country.
During the last war, I was not yet old enough for military service, but despite all this, I did not hesitate to register in the air cadet corps of my country and I acquired in that corps, not education, but the necessary training, that is the training required to help defend my country, if the war had lasted any longer. That is how I know whereof I speak, since I belonged, at an early age, to a military corps which was called the air cadets of Quebec, and this at the Jesuits' college in Quebec.
On the other hand, I think that each individual should be left free to decide. This service should not be imposed upon him, because that is against the democratic principles that we must try to impress upon our young people, instead of trying to impose military service on them or to have them enlist.
Mr. Chairman, those are the remarks I wanted to make about the comments of the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry, and I hope that, in future, the hon. member will think twice before speaking.

Mr. Chairman, may I say that I am sure everybody in this house is conscious of the fact the minister has taken a very searching look at defence. He has been assisted in this by members in all parts of the house who are, I am sure, aiming at precisely the same objectives, that is a more efficient contribution to the security of Canada and to our contributions to the alliance. There is only one thing I would ask the minister, and that is that in his search for economy, for a better role, he very carefully consider what can be done for Canada by those people who have given and who are prepared to give service in our militia.
There was a parade in my riding recently at which almost 100 per cent of the Brock-ville Rifles turned out. These militiamen have been giving hundreds of hours of their time to their country. They have been closely following the proceedings of the defence committee and every statement that has been made by the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order; may I bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that there

are conversations going on in the committee which make it difficult for the Chair to follow the speech now being made.

May I say that these militiamen have been trying to follow intelligently what has been happening. They recognize the high priority of the needs of their fellow Canadians who are serving in the brigade in Europe, in the air force and at sea. They know we have to have new equipment. They know there have to be economies. I am sure this regiment is typical of many regiments across the country, and many hon. members could contribute in relation to their constituencies in the way I am tonight in relation to mine. This regiment has signed a document indicating that 100 per cent of the membership is prepared to continue serving in the regiment without any pay whatsoever. They care very much indeed about the future of the militia.
I know the minister right now is taking the best advice he can get from various sources. I would ask him to consider that the advice he is getting from the service chiefs is, of necessity, placing a high priority on the active forces. These men, who have to choose where cuts may be made in order to replace equipment, do not always find it possible to give the same attention to some factors that they would if the same pressures for economies were not upon them. They cannot now assess the role of the militia as dispassionately and objectively as they otherwise might.
We have had evidence from very distinguished officers such as General Foulkes and General Simonds, both of whom indicated the militia played an important part in the security of Canada. I hope that amongst the people who might be appointed to assist the minister in this advisory capacity there might be a very distinguished soldier, Brigadier Eric Snow, now of Toronto. He has had a lot of experience in action and with the militia. I believe he is the kind of person who will help, because when we are approaching the 100th birthday of Canada I am sure it would be a great tragedy if the militia just disappeared. I am sure the defence committee has not had a chance to go into this matter carefully. I think the minister, with the pressures upon him, has not had a chance to consider this matter with sufficient care.
I am not asking him to make any statement at this time; it would be premature to express a view on this problem. However, some of these militiamen care greatly about Canada and want to play a part in its security. I hope that they will not just go down the drain.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to support what the hon. member for Leeds has said. My whole purpose two weeks ago in declining to pass the estimates then was to give the minister an opportunity to review the situation with regard to the militia and the reserve units of the air force and navy. I was under the impression at the time he made that announcement about cutting the militia almost in half that he was acting rather prematurely. The very fact a person objects to that type of reorganization does not mean that a person is not in favour of reducing expenditures. Of course, the pundits put it the other way around and say that because we object to something the minister has done we are not in favour of reducing these expenditures. This is not the case at all. I imagine the hon. member for Leeds, who has spoken so eloquently about the militia, is just as much in favour of making reductions in defence expenditures as any member in this house. So am I. Surely it is our privilege to suggest to the minister that he re-examine this particular aspect of it and effect the reductions which he requires somewhere else. Let the defence committee assist him in this matter. Had we known that he was going to slice the militia we would most certainly have examined this aspect with great care. We would have had many witnesses there to talk to us. We had no knowledge of this at all until the minister announced it in the house.
The hon. member for Leeds has put forward the case with regard to militia, and the service they give to their country. The minister based part of his argument on the fact the militia is used for general mobilization and that the next war is not going to be like 1914 or 1939. He attempted to leave the impression that I was still thinking in the past. I believe my thinking is away ahead of the minister's. Having served in the militia and in both of these wars, I know very well the militia is not the foundation for general mobilization. How nonsensical to say that
50,000	men in the militia constitutes general mobilization. It is just nonsense. Nowadays we have manning depots for recruiting purposes and for processing people into the service. Having organized and commanded one of these manning depots since the second world war, I know what I am talking about. To say that the present formation of the militia is based in terms of the last world war where great masses of infantry were required is not to understand the facts of history.
In the first world war all sorts of regiments and battalions were organized without a militia foundation whatever. The same is true of the second world war; that is just nonsense. The

Supply-National Defence militia serves a purpose in giving an opportunity to our young men to gain military service. Military service is useful in a young man's life and you do learn things in military service that you do not learn in universities. I have had both experiences. I suggest to the minister that he have another look at this.
I am not overlooking the fact that from time to time the militia of this country has been reorganized. Of course it has. In the period of the '30's a great number of cavalry regiments were disbanded and amalgamations took place. If I had had any influence in the thirties, tank regiments would have been formed. But the thinking of the hierarchy in those days was against anything as modern as a tank. Yet I owe my life to the fact that a tank was present in the first world war. That is how experience influences your thinking. In the '30's the hierarchy was not up to the times. We do not want to be in that position in the '60's. We do not want to be away behind the times, having people in uniform doing jobs for which they are not suited in some future war.
I am prepared to go along with the minister, that the next war is not likely to be one of mass infantry actions, as were the first and second world wars. I am also prepared to go along with the minister that our active forces should be instantly ready for action and properly equipped. Incidentally, I hope the minister will correct Time magazine, which has misquoted him saying that our army is now the best dressed, etc., and the poorest equipped. The minister corrected it in the house, but the Time magazine writer failed to notice that correction.
I am prepared to go along with the minister with regard to the active forces. Behind the active forces, reserve forces are essential. People do move from the reserves to the active forces, and people who retire from the active forces sometimes serve in the reserves. This is true of the army, navy and air force. These reserve forces have some influence on the cadets. There are some changes that may be required; but let us look at them first. To cut the militia in half is to destroy the morale of the militia. I ask for a pause with regard to this proposal.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, let me say this. This was the point raised when we talked about this matter before and I asked the minister about the role of the militia in survival operations in civil defence. I was disappointed that he brushed me off and said this matter would be explained when emergency measures operations were under discussion in the house. Then he said the whole plan apparently had to be revised because the 265 columns for re-entry, and so

on, are either badly placed or are not required in that number. I suggest to the minister that in addition to the work he has to do and the responsibility that rests upon him to make preparation through the services for a thermo-nuclear war, which is the worst of all, for a so-called conventional war and to make preparation for the work that we do with the United Nations, he still has this other job. That is the protection of the civilian population in case another war breaks out. If we are subjected to destruction in Canada by either conventional bombs as used in Europe or thermo-nuclear bombs, such as were used at Hiroshima, then we do need trained, organized, disciplined forces to assist the survivors. I do not know how that could be done except through the assistance of the regular forces and the militia forces that happen to be available in Canada, because people who have training, and understand organization, can assist the willing civilians to do the jobs that are required.
I fail to see how this type of work of survival operations can be carried out by just a civilian organization, because in time of emergency you have to have discipline. The serviceman is disciplined and understands the necessity of obeying orders, whereas the civilian does not have to obey orders. In times of great emergency a firm hand must be used and people must do what they are told. This is the result you get from service people. So, Mr. Chairman, may I join with the hon. member for Leeds in pleading with the minister to postpone his too drastic action with regard to the militia and the reserve units of this country.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a brief question for the minister. It would appear to me that the press and some others have interpreted the minister's recent announcements with regard to defence as reductions in the ultimate expenditures. I would like the minister to clarify that situation and let us know if the result will indeed be a reduction in expenditures or whether it is rather a change of emphasis in the direction of our defence program.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister one question. He may have dealt with this matter already, but I have not the information. Would the minister tell the committee what is planned in connection with navy league cadets, sea cadets and air force cadets, young soldier programs in the militia. Finally, would he tell the committee what will be done with the training divisions at the universities and with regard to training ships such as those in Hamilton, Vancouver and Edmonton-particularly in Edmonton,

where H.M.C.S. Nonsuch has been eliminated. What is to happen to the training division of the University of Alberta?

Mr. Chairman, the details of this are being worked out at the present time. There is no reduction in the allowance for the training of cadets. There was, as I announced on the second day of the debate, a reduction proposed for the future of about 50 per cent of the allowance for the university contingents. How and where the cadets can be housed, however, is a question which will have to be given detailed study. Just as soon as plans are complete, I will be glad to make the hon. gentleman aware of them.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that I did not enter the chamber until about half an hour after the minister started his speech. He may have dealt with this matter, but perhaps he did not. I would like to ask the minister if, as Minister of National Defence, he can in any way take this house into his confidence and give us some indication as to any proposals he may have made to the NATO council as to the role of Canada's armed forces within the operations of NATO.

Mr. Chairman, I think I did give the committee all the information that I can give at this time in that respect. There were no new proposals put forward to the council beyond the readjustment of the air division, which was referred to previously.

In the absence of the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay), who should take interest in this situation, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence, in connection with the low level of employment in the Canadian shipyards and especially in those of Lauzon.
Could the minister tell us whether the contract relating to the building of three submarines, which was awarded to shipyards in Great Britain, was awarded for economic or for technical reasons?

Mr. Chairman, the answer to this question has been given a number of times in the house. It was a production sharing arrangement which was really commenced by the previous government and which this government decided to carry on. It does not actually involve a loss of employment to Canada. What it does mean is a shift in employment from one industry to another. This has a detrimental effect in one area and a beneficial effect in another. In order to alleviate the situation temporarily, the government has already announced a shipbuilding program in the civilian field. Beyond that, the 28902-5-398J
Supply-National Defence Department of National Defence has indicated that it will resume its shipbuilding program just as soon as it possibly can, following certain studies which are now being carried out. The shipbuilding program will be a Canadian program, and the future requirements of the Royal Canadian Navy will be built in Canadian shipyards.
Would the minister answer my question?

I do not think I am at liberty
to give the proposed estimates of our department for next year, but in the debate a week ago I said it was our intention to hold expenditures at about the current level and at the same time have a change of emphasis, to shift some of our expenditures from operations and maintenance to capital, to permit more research development and construction of new equipment.
Am I right in assuming we could not expect a reduction in expenditures, but just a change of emphasis?
That depends. A reduction from what? What is your starting point?

We all sympathize with the minister in the job he has to do and we realize adjustments and re-evaluation of programs are necessary, but I know that during the past three years the Saskatchewan area command has a new morale compared with its previous low morale, which resulted from an unfortunate situation that developed in previous years when the militia were somewhat downgraded. There has been a considerable pick up in the last three or four years. We are all proud of the new esprit de corps and the revitalization of the area command, our militia unit, and H.M.C.S. Queen which has given service for 40 years.
Among many people there has been great concern that the minister's initial announcement was too hasty and the evolution of the new program was not considered fully. I believe the minister has received some representations from Regina, and I wonder has he replied promising reconsideration, especially with regard to H.M.C.S. Queen?

I have not given any specific undertakings. What I have suggested is that this does not mean the end to the militia. Quite the contrary. Although we will have a smaller reserve force I am sure it will be a more effective force. I am sure there is general agreement that though at the moment we have quite a large number of units, some rethinking as to the number of units and the groupings should be undertaken.
That is the reason we are seeking assistance in this case from militiamen who know the

Supply-National Defence
history, effectiveness and capabilities of the militia units. We will indicate to them what we need, the requirements we have for reserve forces, what they are to undertake and what their responsibilities will be. Then we will expect them to assist us by making recommendations for reorganization which will provide effective reserve units to carry out the tasks which would be theirs. Although this will mean a reduction in the numbers,
I am sure the total force if anything will be more effective.
Is any reconsideration being given to the announcement that H.M.C.S. Queen would be closed completely and abandoned?
I do not think it has been reconsidered.

This is a department which concerns our party very much, but in view of the fact that the minister is taking a completely new look at all aspects of the armed services, that he has announced he will be bringing down a white paper early next year, that the special committee on defence has filed an interim report and hopes to be able to continue its studies next session, so far as I am concerned I have no more to say at this stage; but I want it clearly understood that this is on the basis of the white paper, the interim report, and the continuation of the study by the defence committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not have very much more to say but I am surprised the minister is so assured his proposed reorganization of the militia is the right thing. He tells us the militia force will be cut in half, and then the militia officers will be called together to inform him whose throat is to be cut and which regiment. He says he is convinced we will have a much more efficient operation, but there is no evidence on which to base this point of view. I would like to ask the minister, who perhaps has not been associated with the militia-I am not sure-what happens if you cut the militia down to half size? Will the militia units only be in the big cities? What about all the smaller villages and towns from which have been drawn some of the best fighting men in Canadian history?
I could give many an instance of the work that has been done by militiamen and by retired soldiers. I can tell him of a retired naval chap who worked with the reserve army for years in an area in Manitoba which has produced, on a percentage basis, more men for the services than any other part of Canada. The reserve force was essential in order to give the young men something to do. If the forces are to be cut in half, will they be located in the big cities, or outside them

in smaller places? It seems to me this cannot be done. We are talking in terms of
50,000	men scattered across 10 provinces, and that is a very small percentage of the population.
Like the hon. member for Leeds I wonder whether the minister has been listening to some people who scoff at the militia and think of them as "Saturday night soldiers," as they were described in a recent Time article. The Saturday night soldiers have given every whit as good service in times of emergency as others.
Has the minister been talking to some regular officers who are a bit irritated with the duties revolving upon them because of the militia? I have been all through this, and I understand the thinking of some people in the regular services who find it a bit troublesome working with a militia unit. From what source is he getting his advice. He cannot expect us to accept his assurance that this plan will provide a more efficient and better reserve force. That is not logical and I suggest he put a stop order on the so-called reorganization of the militia and the reserve units.
Let him give this problem to the defence committee for study, if that committee is reconstituted next session. It is too easy to write off the militia, and I speak from experience. I recall in 1938 when the crisis was almost upon us, at the time of Munich, a friend of mine said, "Now, you fellows who have been playing at soldiers, here is your chance." That was the way some civilians looked at the people who were in the militia. Our chance came one year later in 1939. They were Saturday night soldiers, says someone who I bet has never served in uniform. No one who had served in uniform would speak so disparagingly of the militia of this country. These people who have not given service say: "Well, these are just social clubs". Mr. Chairman, you can spend three nights a week in militia, as I have done year after year. That is why I did not become a first-class curler in the wintertime, because I spent three nights a week for many years on militia work. That was no social club activity. That was not being a Saturday night soldier. It was attempting to do something for our country, and a great many other people across the land did the same thing. I did not do anything of any special importance; others have done much more.
The militia of this country has never been properly recognized, and I think the minister has taken the wrong advice on this matter. However, I want to save him for another day. Let us save him for some other larger problems which we can quarrel over more effectively. Let us not quarrel over the militia.

Let the minister recognize the militia as the force it is in this country, and keep it in being, with certain modifications of course, without slicing it in half. What has disturbed us over the minister's action is the tremendous slice cut out of the militia. If it had been a proposed reorganization plan with a smaller percentage cut it would be different; but to cut the amount almost in half I think is disturbing and, I say seriously, is very unwise.

Mr. Chairman, about the radar station in my riding. I am duty bound to intervene, because I have received from almost all the municipal councils to be found in the constituency of Lotbiniere a resolution stressing the importance of maintaining the radar station in St. Sylvestre. The chief reason for doing so is that the 80 civil servants who are working there would be laid off if the station were to be closed.
Mr. Chairman, I am strongly in favour of defence cutbacks. In this regard, I must pay special tribute to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) for acting the way he did.
However, I do not think it is expedient to close the radar station unless air detection has made such progress that it is no longer needed. If the rumours going around are true, then I believe it is my duty to urge the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and the Minister of National Defence to see that none of those employees will be laid off and that the station is not closed before jobs have been found for those people.

Mr. Chairman, I have one comment before leaving this item. It arises from the reply given by the minister. I hope that our civil defence program is not to be crippled so as to acquire high-priced hardware. When you take into consideration the situation in the world today, you cannot do justice to the subject at this time. In view of the state of the session I do not want to say anything more. However, I do want to leave that thought with the minister if he is bringing forward new programs.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This completes the estimates of the Department of National Defence.

Mr. Chairman, if you will just permit me before we go on to the next item of business I should like to thank the committee for its co-operation not only today but during the two earlier days of debate. I was very pleased with the quality of the
Supp ly-Transport
debate. I found it very interesting and helpful and I think it reflected the study given of the matter by the special committee on defence. While I am mentioning the special committee on defence, I should just like to compliment that committee, the members of it individually and collectively, on the excellent report which they presented to the house today. They have obviously taken their task very seriously and worked assiduously in order to come up with a consensus which I believe represents a very good judgment of the evidence and the opinions put before them.
While I was in Europe last week I received only the highest praise and compliments, not only for the deportment of the committee when visiting Europe but also for the way they attacked their tasks and the intelligent and searching questions which they put forward. There is no question that over the past few years there has been a considerable amount of emotionalism regarding defence problems in this country. The report of the committee today represents, in my opinion, a tendency or trend toward, a non-partisan or multi-partisan approach to defence prob-blems. I think this is a most rewarding development. It was well worth the effort, because in my opinion defence is much too serious a business to be the subject of political footballing. I was very pleased to see the report and I congratulate the committee on their work. I am sure that, if the committee is reconstituted in the next session, it will carry on with many of the worth-while studies it has undertaken during this session.

120. Railway employees' provident fund-to supplement pension allowances under the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees' Provident Fund Act so as to make the minimum allowance payable in the calendar year 1963 $30 per month instead of $20 per month as fixed by the said act, $7,000.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the last time we were dealing with the estimates of the Department of Transport I had a few subjects on which I wanted the minister to comment. Certain items were allowed to stand in order that he might be able to speak to us on these particular subjects. Item 120, I think the minister indicated, was an appropriate item under which he would deal with the question of necessary improvements in pensions of retired employees of the Canadian National Railways, and I hope the minister is ready with an appropriate statement on this subject tonight.
The minister knows that members of all parties in the house have for many years raised questions regarding the pensions of Canadien National Railways employees. We

Supply-Transport
are all aware of the fact that about a year and a half ago some very significant improvements were made in the pension plan so far as those still in service were concerned. I am raising this question because I want an answer from the minister and I do not see any point in talking if other people are talking to him over there.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Which minister?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The Minister of Transport.
He is listening, now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Good. The point I was trying to make is that improvements in the pensions paid by the Canadian National Railways were made in the early part of 1962 by a revision of the plan, as far as those still in the company's service are concerned. But no improvements have been made affecting those who retired before April 1, 1962.
A few years ago, whenever we argued in favour of improving the pensions of employees of the C.N.R. or of retired civil servants, or of any group of people who had already retired, we were met with the argument that there had been a contractual arrangement and nothing could be done. But, as the minister knows, improvements have been made in the pensions of retired civil servants. Some of us think it is about time that these improvements were brought up to date; but at least the principle has been established. Some private employers have also recognized this problem and made increases in the pensions of employees already retired. The minister knows that there has been a great deal of correspondence about this subject throughout the years. Some of us feel it has been most unfortunate that these men who served the company for many years should not be getting the benefit of the higher standard of living and the higher standard of pensions which is now more general. Just as the company in co-operation with the government was able to meet the needs of those still in the service of the railway, I hope the government and the railway will find a way to deal with the pensions of those who retired prior to April 1, 1962.
The minister knows, because we have both been in this house for a good many years, that sometimes when I have made this plea I have trotted out the statistics which the minister of the day has put on record in Hansard in response to my questions. Those statistics indicate the number of retired railway workers who receive pensions and the amounts of pension they receive. Certainly, the number who receive pensions at a very low figure is altogether too high. I know this can be explained. In fact, in the tables which are given in Hansard there is usually

a footnote explaining them. The fact remains that these faithful servants of bygone years are among those who have been overlooked with regard to the improvements which have been made for retired people generally. I hope we can hear from the minister on this important subject, and maybe tonight he will have something encouraging to tell the committee with regard to it.

As the hon. member has correctly stated, this subject was dealt with about a year and a half ago. As a result, those who are still employed are in a much better position with regard to their pensions. But the people who are of concern to the hon. member are those who retired before, and I take it he is concerned to know whether or not the government has any measure to bring forward at this time or in the immediate future which would better their conditions. I do not think this is an oversimplification of the hon. member's submission.
I want to tell him it is quite wrong of him to say that these persons have been overlooked. At the time I am not able to give the hon. member any helpful information with respect to them. It is a complicated question. It means providing, from one side only, funds out of which to pay the additional pensions. It involves, by inference, raising the pensions of all others as well. It would involve the railways bringing a plan forward. I assume, bearing in mind the operational requirements of the railways and the desirability of keeping costs down, that it would involve looking to the government for the funds from which to pay the increases suggested and I regret to tell the hon. member I am not able to give him any encouraging news at the moment.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: In view of the minister's statement that he has no encouraging news to give the committee on this subject I wonder what he means by saying that these retired employees have not been overlooked. It seems to me they have been overlooked and are still being overlooked.

That is not my understanding of the language. What it means is that this question has been getting attention. It has been studied. As I may have put on record -or perhaps it was something I said in private conversation-this very subject is receiving some study now and I hope to have these studies continued with a view to seeing whether something could be done. But there is nothing of a definite nature which I can say which would be helpful, and I am one who does not believe in trying to create a more favourable picture than that which actually exists.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
If the minister had only said that the matter was being studied I suppose we could take some hope out of it, but when he adds those words about nothing definite being under consideration it is a bleak prospect for the people concerned. I do not think it is enough to say that this is a complicated business, that it involves finding the money, and so on. I have already reminded the hon. gentleman of what had been done for retired civil servants up to a certain point in time. This was done on the basis of a formula worked out, although it had been said year after year that it was a complicated matter and that it could not be dealt with. I would remind him that the item under which we are having this discussion, an item which has been in the estimates for many years, provides for a supplement to the pensions of employees who came under the old Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees Provident Fund Act-pensions which according to that original act were very low. Yet some of these people are still alive, and it was recognized, on an ex gratia basis if you will, that they were entitled to something better.
And so a method was found. This item decreases year by year as these men advance in years and leave us. However, there are these several examples of a way being found when there is a will to find it. The minister says he has no good news to give me or the men concerned, but I hope the little sentence he put in about the matter being studied is one which will be stepped up. He must know from experience that some of us, when we feel we have a case that is just, do not let go. It is not just a case of making the same request year after year for the sake of hearing ourselves talk. It is also because we are aware of the fact that some of these cases that for 10 or 15 or 20 years we thought we could never win have eventually been won. I believe that the retired Canadian National employees who are asking that something be done for them have a just cause, and I hope the minister will step up the study or, to use the modern phrase, that he will do a study in depth and find a way to deal with the complications and to get the money, so that these retired faithful servants of the Canadian National Railways may enjoy the pension standards that are possible today.

Item agreed to.
