Mr. Chairman, I just have one or two brief questions to ask the minister on this vote. They concern the matter of sums to be repaid to international air lines
Supply-Transport
as a result of the withdrawal of the government's suit against Pan American and KLM in connection with overflight charges that were made. Would the minister inform the committee what the total amount of repayments to the international air lines was, and would he also indicate specifically the amounts repaid to each of the air lines concerned?

Mr. Chairman, it is not possible to give that information because the precise amounts have not been calculated. This is an individual matter that has to be worked out with each air line, and because of the effect of allowances for other charges and so on the information is just not available yet. In any event, I can tell the hon. member that the total amount is something over $1 million.

Mr. Chairman, I think the committee is entitled to more specific information than that. As I understand government accounting procedures, moneys received by the government are accounted for properly. Receipts are issued upon the receipt of any sums by the department, and proper bookkeeping entries are made. Therefore it should not be difficult at all to determine immediately what amount is owing to each of the international air lines concerned. The reason I raise the question is that I doubt very much whether the minister knows.
He does.
If the minister knows, surely he can inform the committee what amounts are due and owing to the air lines involved.

I can only repeat that with the way the various charges applicable to air lines of this type are set out there may be deductions, in that when one charge is paid another one does not become payable and so on. The consequence is that you have to take each air line individually, get their flight statements and then re-account for a whole series of charges on each flight statement and arrive at the amount. This is now in the course of being worked out with the individual air lines. This being so, it is not possible to give the precise amount because it has not been determined by the department or, indeed, by the air lines themselves; but the best estimate I can give of the total amount to be repaid is a little over $1 million.

I still feel that the committee is entitled to a more satisfactory reply than the minister has given. If the minister knows the total amount of moneys that have been paid by these international air lines it should not be difficult at all to delineate specifically the exact sums which are due to be returned

Supply-Transport
to these international air lines as a result of the withdrawal of the suits against the two concerned. I believe the department does not know at all the precise amounts that are owing to the air lines. 1 believe further that the departmental officials-I was going to say the minister but perhaps it happened before his time-actually had to communicate with the air lines concerned to ask them how much money they had paid in. In other words, the government had to rely on the bookkeeping of the air lines in order to determine the amounts that were owing.
I am sure the committee would be very pleased to have the minister's reassurance that this was not the case. In any event, government accounting procedures surely are sufficiently precise to allow the minister to give a specific answer to this question, because this business of paying money in and paying money out as explained by the minister does not get around the fact that ordinary acceptable bookkeeping practices should be sufficiently accurate to allow the minister to state with precision the exact amounts that are owing to the air lines concerned.

As I indicated earlier, certain charges are not made where overflight charges have been made. For instance, a landing fee is not payable. Therefore you have to recompute the charge made on each flight. Each one has to be recomputed. What has been done represents a little more care in the accounting and bookkeeping system than the standard the hon. member is seeking to have imposed, in that the government sought to check and cross-check every figure with the companies concerned so there would be no dispute afterwards. In effect you have full knowledge, because you have the benefit of the cross-check. That is why the companies were asked for that information and I think it is the correct way to proceed in the matter. That is what I meant to indicate.
Is the minister saying that the department actually communicated with the air lines concerned in order to ask them how much they had paid to the department in respect of these overflight charges?
No, Mr. Chairman, but the department did communicate with each air line to cross-check their records.

On this point I wonder whether the minister communicated with Trans-Canada Air Lines for the same purpose, in order to determine whether or not the figures that the minister mentioned were accurate with respect to that international air line?
In the case of every trans-Canada flight, they were landing in Canada so it would not be necessary with them.

Am I to take it that Trans-Canada Air Lines as an international carrier paid no overflight fees at all under the Financial Administration Act which authorized the charging of fees against two international air lines using Canadian air space, and air space under Canadian jurisdiction?
That statement I believe to be correct. It is possible there could have been a flight or two but I believe the statement to be correct.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I have to reiterate that the members of this group have always been strong supporters of Trans-Canada Air Lines. We have always believed that the best air transportation system in Canada should be publicly owned. We certainly opposed the decision of the former government to permit C.P.A. to operate a transcontinental run, a decision which has since caused T.C.A. financial difficulties. It is with a good deal of regret, therefore, that I want to say that some of us are, to say the least, very unhappy about the leadership that T.C.A. is getting from its present chief officers. We do not like to criticize the detailed operations of a crown corporation. I am not rising to complain about Mr. McGregor just because I disagree with a decision he obviously made some years ago that the head office and most of the operations of T.C.A. which had been in Winnipeg should be moved to Montreal.
If Mr. McGregor had had the approval of his board of directors, if he had so reported to the government and to the minister in charge, and the minister had reported to parliament and had received approval for this transfer, even though it was and is a real blow to the city of Winnipeg, I would not now be complaining. The fact is that on innumerable occasions Mr. McGregor speaking for T.C.A., as well as the ministers in charge-

I was saying that if this decision of T.C.A. to move the major facilities from Winnipeg to Montreal had been made years ago, and had been approved by parliament, I would not be objecting. As I said, the fact that the decision had been made has been denied consistently. As long ago as 1948 questions were asked about the possibility of this move of T.C.A.'s head office from Winnipeg to Montreal. The minister then in charge, the late C. D. Howe, made it very clear T.C.A. had no intention of moving its main departments from Winnipeg. I was not here when Mr. Howe was minister, but I have heard enough about him and read enough to know that he was a pretty strong minister. If it had been recommended to him by T.C.A. that the headquarters should be moved, if the case had been proved to him, he would have so reported to the house. I do not believe for a moment, Mr. Chairman, that Mr. Howe would have said in 1948 that there was no intention to do this, if the decision had been made and he had known about it.
At that time Mr. Howe said that while some head office departments might be moved, 95 per cent of the company's activities would remain centered in Winnipeg. A few months later, following further rumours that T.C.A. would move its main overhaul base to Montreal, Mr. Gordon McGregor, then as now T.C.A. president, said that some executive staff might move but the overhaul base would stay. In 1949, Mr. McGregor announced that the administrative offices and operations department of T.C.A. would move to Montreal in the fall. He said, and I quote:
-there is no conceivable reason nor any grounds for suspicion that this move marks the beginning of a mass transfer of T.C.A. activities to Montreal.
Later that year Mr. Howe said that T.C.A. did not contemplate making further transfers of personnel from Winnipeg to other centres. In October, 1951, T.C.A. transferred radio
28902-5-399
Supply-Transport
technicians to Montreal. In the same month a T.C.A. official said there was never any suggestion that the mechanical operations of the company would be moved from Winnipeg and that the city would continue to house the system's only complete repair system. In February, 1956, T.C.A. announced that it was dropping major overhaul work on aircraft radio equipment in Winnipeg, and that the staff had been offered transfers to Montreal where the work was to be centralized.
A few months later Mr. McGregor denied that the company was about to consolidate its two repair depots at Montreal and Winnipeg into one unit. In September, 1957, T.C.A. officials denied rumours that the overhaul base was to be moved from Winnipeg. Mr. McGregor assured T.C.A. employees in Winnipeg that operations in the city would not be curtailed as new operations were introduced. In October 1958 a T.C.A. official announced that in 1960 T.C.A. would move another 100 of its Winnipeg based workers to Montreal. This was the instrument shop.
In January, 1961, Mr. Hees, then the minister in charge, wrote a letter to the Manitoba government to the effect that the overhaul base in Winnipeg would be closed in 1965 or shortly thereafter.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in January of this year, I think it was, the people of Manitoba sent a delegation to see the government. The then minister, Mr. Balcer, assured them that a study would be made and that in the meantime there would be a job freeze as far as Winnipeg was concerned. During the election campaign the present Prime Minister made certain statements. I am not going to go into them tonight because we can debate them at some other time. These statements were taken by everybody in Winnipeg, including the Liberal candidate in the last federal election, and the Winnipeg Free Press, as a commitment that Winnipeg would remain the major overhaul base for T.C.A. I believe that in June another delegation from Manitoba came to see the Prime Minister and he gave the same assurance. The other day the Prime Minister reiterated the same kind of thing in a statement to another delegation.
The overhaul base at present is overhauling the Viscount and Vanguard planes which, as soon as T.C.A. switches to medium jets, will no longer be used. Obviously, then, the base will have to be closed. The interesting thing, and the obvious thing is that since January, when supposedly we were to have a job freeze promised by the former government, and which I take it is still in effect because this government has not repudiated it, 200 workers at the overhaul base have been transferred to Montreal. There are now 200 jobs less in Winnipeg than there were in

Supply-Transport
January. I do not think this is an accident. I think this is part of a deliberate plan made by Mr. McGregor of T.C.A. back in the late forties. If T.C.A. had given reasons for this decision at that time, I might have disagreed with it, but I would not be objecting now.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that this has been done by stealth, with deliberate misrepresentation by Mr. McGregor. When I say that I want to say that I speak for every group in Winnipeg, every political party, every trade union and every business organization in Manitoba. Indeed, I can honestly say I have never seen such united feeling on any issue as I have on this. In my opinion, when the head of a crown corporation misrepresents the facts as Mr. McGregor has, when he hides important matters from the people who hired him, because after all T.C.A. belongs to the people of Canada, that man has outlived his usefulness. Mr. Chairman, I think it is time the government gave serious consideration to getting a new president for T.C.A.

Mr. Chairman, since item 140 refers to civil aviation, as a member of this house, I should like to call the Minister of Transport's attention to an important point.
I would like to know whether the Minister of Transport, who is responsible after all for civil aviation and its related branches in Canada, or his departmental officials, makes investigations and experiments in order to develop a true aeronautics industry in Canada.
This is a question of current interest, since T.C.A. has purchased or will purchase over a rather brief period about 30 rather large aircraft as well as medium range jets.
There is then good ground to ask ourselves whether a crown corporation directly coming under the Department of Transport and with the assistance of other departments of the government and with all our engineers, technicians, labourers, could not have promoted the permanent establishment of such an important industry in our country, such as the aeronautics industry? Is the government taking the necessary steps to achieve that purpose?
It is noted that T.C.A. has chosen an aircraft, a very unimportant part of which furthermore will be manufactured in Canada, while this opportunity could have been used to undertake the development of a complete aeronautics industry.
We feel that the Minister of Transport is to blame in that connection for failing to intervene and protect the interests of the Canadian people and to develop our aircraft industry.

We put on the order paper a motion calling for the tabling of the report submitted by T.C.A. employees, engineers and experts concerning the choice of the new aircraft. Our request was turned down and the main argument used to justify the choice of the DC-9 is that its operation would be cheaper for T.C.A. It may well be; in fact, we are quite ready to admit it.
In that case, only T.C.A. would be making savings. Would it not have been possible to consider savings at other administrative levels? Would it not have been possible to prove that the savings made by T.C.A. could have resulted in much bigger savings for the country?
If you consider the question in general, the choice of the DC-9 means that T.C.A. will be buying an American aircraft. That is a serious business since our capital will be flowing out of the country at a time when our balance of payments is already unfavourable.
Had we been in a position to decrease the deficit balance of our international payments by that much, I am sure that the Minister of Finance, if he were here, would have been very glad. This is to say that we would have been able to make direct savings in that the balance of our deficit payments would have been reduced by that much. We would have thus had a certain profit which could have made up for the savings that T.C.A. has been able to make by purchasing the DC-9 aircraft.
The second factor is the fact that the DC-9 will be mostly built in the United States, while we could have built the Caravelle in Canada. This would have supplied work for many years to thousands of Canadians, and would have resulted in another saving, in that those workers pay income tax to the Canadian government.
Now as a third element; we must consider the expenses it would have saved the Canadian government, namely that the government would have avoided paying unemployment insurance or social assistance benefits to every one of those unemployed. It would already be a second source of savings that the Canadian government would have made on the whole.
It is a fact that when two Canadian workers are given jobs in industry, a third Canadian citizen finds employment in related spheres or in sales. That means that for every
2,000	Canadian citizens employed in the building of the Caravelle we would have 1,000 Canadian citizens employed in related fields of services or sales.
Then if we consider the salaries paid to Canadians, if we consider the taxes paid to the government by Canadians, if we consider unemployment insurance and social welfare,

that the government does not have to pay if we consider the savings realized by the Minister of Finance in reducing our balance of payments, then we can realize that for the country as a whole, it might have been more profitable if Trans-Canada Air Lines had got these Caravelle aircrafts, even at a greater expense.
In my opinion, the Minister of Transport, as a responsible member of the federal cabinet, should have tabled this report and submit it to the members of the house and to the other members of the cabinet, in an attempt to find out whether, on the whole, it would not have been possible to save more money than by purchasing the DC-9.
All the more so since at the present time any industry could have developed. We could have trained technicians, skilled workers who could have created a Canadian aircraft industry. There is no doubt that would have helped our country to find new markets, new export outlets.
If we had wanted to study the problem, not only in the limited sense of technicians and experts, but adding to it a number of opinions, the views of our competent economists-at least those who are-we could have studied also the problem of industry and foreign trade as well as our balance of payments deficit. Those are all matters T.C.A. could have looked into.
The Minister of Transport has neither the character, nor the strength or competence required in that field to analyse all the related problems concerning the choice of an aircraft. In fact, he has not even shown the business ability which we expect to find not only with a director of a crown corporation but with a member of the cabinet of a country like Canada which is due to develop. Mr. Chairman, that is the point I wanted to bring up.
There is also another field in which the Minister of Transport must assume his part of responsibilities as he was sitting beside the president of T.C.A. when the latter made his statements on the Caravelle, the aircraft produced by the Sud-Aviation.
I have read the committee's report on that point. Sometimes I feel that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), have some responsibilities in the matter, and that they must try and restore the harmony which should reign between two great countries like Canada and France, and between two large air companies like Canadair and Sud-Aviation.
I think that the minister should see to it that the necessary excuses are offered to the French people, who are a proud people and

Supply-Transport
naturally keen about a plane like the Caravelle, which has been imitated by several other countries.
I hear the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) saying, ah! ah!; I feel sure that his constituents, many of whom will not be able to find jobs, because the member for Dollard did not have the courage to stand up and to demand that the Caravelle be built in Montreal-
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he know that the 5,800 employees of Canadair will hold their jobs for two more years because of the contracts awarded by the federal government?

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate what the hon. member for Dollard has just said, but I never learned to be satisfied with little when I can get much more. If the hon. member for Dollard is satisfied with the minimum, his electors will judge him, but as far as I am concerned, I think that a country like Canada, in the full swing of 20th century development, cannot be satisfied with the minimum but should rather strive for continuous development and for increasingly accelerated progress. It is nice to be satisfied with the minimum, but the Canadian people need better members than that; they need members who want their country to have an aircraft industry as well as develop and prosper in all other fields.
Mr. Chairman, as I was saying, apologies should be tendered. I said also that we should get more information on those matters and above all inform the people because today they want to know what is behind all those things.
When, for instance, a report published about the Winnipeg base, which was mentioned in the house, says not only that this base must not be closed but should be kept in operation until 1973 and, a little later, it is said that an aircraft built in the United States must be purchased and the minister then refuses to consider instances and requests made to him in favour of another aircraft, we think there is one law for the rich and one for the poor.
If the minister had analysed the whole situation, not only on the basis of T.C.A. but on the basis rather of the general economy of the country, I am convinced that changes would have been made at that time and that we would have agreed to build an aircraft called Caravelle thus developing an aircraft industry here in our country which would have provided jobs for our people.
Mr. Chairman, I said earlier, when the hon. member for Dollard interrupted me, that we should offer apologies to the French people who are proud of their Caravelle which is

Supply-Transport
today copied by several other aircraft designers in other countries, and among them the builders of the DC-9 who are using the same fundamental principles which was used by the French aircraft industry when it built its Caravelle and even its Super-Caravelle. The latter will be more technically advanced and will be put into service, not in ten years as has been claimed, but in 1964 as asserted by Sud-Aviation.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that those are important points which have not been taken into consideration lately and on which the cabinet did not try to get information. But I say that this must be a warning to the present cabinet, and that the facts must be put forth so that, when faced by a problem, it does not approach it in such a restricted sense but in a sense that embraces the whole economy and development of the country.

Before this item passes I want to ask the minister a question to which I hope he can give me a satisfactory answer. What considerations were given by T.C.A. to Transair in return for the latter company assuming responsibility for the so-called prairie milk run? The reason I ask the question is that, as most hon. members know, T.C.A. found the prairie milk run uneconomic and wanted to dispose of it. Transair offered to take it over and applied for the franchise.
I am told that the consideration given to Transair by T.C.A. consisted of a Viscount, two DC-3 aircraft, and about $500,000 worth of DC-3 aircraft parts, all for the nominal sum of $1. In the committee the president of T.C.A. said this was a good deal for T.C.A. because it was getting out of an uneconomic line. I am not quarrelling with the deal at all. The reason I am raising the question is that Transair, who got this very considerable reimbursement, has now applied to get out of the uneconomic parts of the prairie milk run, and under air transport board order No. 3784 of December 10, 1963, they are going to abandon the service from Regina, Swift Current, Medicine Hat and Calgary, effective January 11, 1964.
The point I am making is that this company got a very considerable compensation to assume a franchise on the prairies, and it would appear it is now welching on the agreement; that having got some consideration from T.C.A. it is now prepared to drop the uneconomic part of the run, retain the lucrative part of the operation, and still keep whatever consideration T.C.A. gave it. I am not blaming the minister. This did not come under him, but what I am asking is whether T.C.A. is going to recover any part of what was given to Transair, or is the air transport

board going to take into consideration, when it reviews this matter, that this company not only applied for a franchise and got it, but got in addition a very considerable reimbursement in the form of the aircraft and the $500,000 worth of parts to which I have referred?
I would like to ask the minister what consideration was given? Is the consideration I have outlined an accurate one, and what steps is the government going to take to make sure that Transair, having accepted this consideration, is not now going to be allowed to welch on its agreement and discontinue the service which it undertook to operate when it applied for the franchise and took this consideration from T.C.A.?
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to speak for too long-
Hear, hear.

-in view of the enthusiastic reception I am getting from my hon. friends opposite, I shall stretch my comments.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to refer to certain articles which have appeared in the press, especially one written by a talented young writer, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), concerning the dealings of the French ambassador to Canada. The Ottawa correspondent of the Winnipeg Free Press also wrote on the same subject.
Mr. Chairman, I believe everything the French ambassador did in this matter was right. I know that some people, like the hon. member for Port Arthur, were shocked because the ambassasor of another country tried to help one of his country's industries to secure a contract in Canada. In my opinion, there is absolutely nothing there that is not in keeping with the role of an ambassador and I would go as far as to say that all good ambassadors are guilty of the same crime. Besides, the duties of an ambassador have evolved considerably in past years, especially since we have international organizations, like the United Nations and NATO, and since communications between countries take place at the ministerial level when political questions are settled directly between governments.
In my opinion, the embassy in question accomplished its duty by trying to promote, quite strongly, I must admit, the sale of a national product. I have nothing to say against that and, moreover, I hope our Canadian ambassadors will do the same thing everywhere in the world, instead of just giving parties.
I may quote the example of one of our best ambassadors, Mr. Bull, who was ambassador at Tokyo. I recall that once every year he

would give a party for all the bakers in the city of Tokyo, in order to promote the sale of good Canadian wheat. I suggest that this ambassador acted as a good Canadian and that he did not do anything not in keeping with his duties as an ambassador, even if he did not follow the old obsolete rules which may have had some purpose in the past. I believe that in doing what he did Mr. Bull played his role of a Canadian representative abroad.
Now, I should like to tell my hon. friend from Port Arthur that, instead of being shocked because a foreign ambassador behaves like a good citizen of his country, he should write another article, in that style of his we all marvel at, where he would encourage our own ambassadors to do the same.

I should like to ask the hon. member a question. Can he explain, if this is good tactics-and I am not going to quarrel with that particular argument-why there was none of the propaganda in favour of the Caravelle put to the English speaking members of parliament? Does this not raise the issue that there is a possibility that the French ambassador, recognizing a particularly difficult situation in the country at this time, was deliberately exploiting the kind of spirit which is tending to divide us?

The hon. member for Port Arthur was a member of the committee, as I was, and I think he was the one who asked, or was there when one of the members asked, the Minister of Transport whether he had received a visit from General Puget of Sud-Aviation. He asked the minister who was accompanying General Puget and the minister said that it was the French ambassador. The French ambassador addressed himself to the Minister of Transport. He was very friendly to the French Canadians, but he is not a French Canadian. I do not know about the different moves which have been made by the French ambassador, but I think that by addressing himself to the Minister of Transport he has done precisely what my hon. friend was trying to say that he did not do. I do not know everything that the French ambassador did, but I would not be at all scandalized if he tried to sell a product of his country. I hope our ambassadors will do this same thing, wherever they are in the world.

Mr. Chairman, I will take only a few minutes to raise a couple of points. One arises out of the hearings of the committee dealing with T.C.A., wherein I found it a little dismaying to find that the Montreal-Ottawa-Toronto run is losing so much money. On this run aircraft are operating at a very
Supply-Transport
satisfactory level of occupancy. The testimony before the committee indicated that under apparently ideal conditions of passenger traffic in the present aircraft, or on the DC19 which they are planning to buy, all we could look forward to is a further deficit on this run. Since the public will have to reimburse any deficit, what dismays me is that there was no testimony given to show what plans T.C.A. have to circumvent this problem. There was no suggestion of a new way to cut overhead.
By way of example, let me take the P.W.A. air bus between Edmonton and Calgary, on which run you merely walk on the plane and buy your passage on the aircraft. This might be more appropriate under item 145, dealing with ground handling, etc. It might also mean that T.C.A have some ideas which they did not reveal to the committee, although I wish they had said something about it.
So far as our last meeting was concerned, the situation seemed to be that with a satisfactory volume of traffic to create maximum efficiency, and with the aircraft of their choice, they cannot operate a run of that kind with anything but a deficit for some time to come in the future. The committee was left in this state, that there was no suggestion from T.C.A. that they had used any imagination as to different aircraft, a different manner of handling them, or any method of reducing ground handling costs or other costs, or whether the run should be taken over by a smaller air line with a smaller overhead. Perhaps that is the answer, but I want to inform the minister of the situation as it exists today.
It is not so bad where T.C.A. does provide a much needed service. It is not a case where they cannot get the passenger traffic. They have a very satisfactory passenger demand. In cases where planes are full but they are still losing money, obviously something more is needed. If T.C.A. have no more answers they had better find them, and I hope it is not a case of concealment from the committee.
Another point concerns Edmonton municipal airport, a matter I have raised before. The present situation is that half the traffic out of Edmonton use the new Niksu airport and half the old municipal airport, but the government is cutting off some assistance, less than $200,000 a year. If the municipal airport is cut down in this way the result to Edmonton is a loss of service. The planes now flying from the Nisku airport to Calgary are not giving as good a service as they used to give. We have made a very large investment, and if there is discouragement of air services at the municipal airport about 50 per cent of Edmonton's present air services

Supply-Transport
are going to step down a grade again. I think that no one in authority would want to think that the immediate result of an investment of $30 million or more on a new airport is a reduction in air services. The proposed reduction of $200,000 a year is less than one half of the interest on the money invested. This seems to me a penny wise, pound foolish approach. If government expenditures on airports and air services are justified we must strive to get the most per dollar we can. I want to point out that the dollars which go the furthest and give the most in air services, and the most to Edmonton, Calgary and the entire north country as far as the Edmonton municipal airport is concerned, are those dollars now spent on the municipal airport at Edmonton. I ask the minister to reflect seriously before he cuts out this small amount of money and gives Edmonton a worse air service than it had before. At the moment, the only benefit we have is from the jets. Long range jets can land there. But most of the service at that airport has been poorer, and if the department continues its present policy the other half of the air service will deteriorate. The minister can stop this trend, if he wishes, by restoring the cut and making sure that Edmonton airport remains open and that we can have good service.

Mr. Chairman, I fully agree with the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) concerning the statement made by the hon. gentleman for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher).
I think the French ambassador to Canada was duty-bound to take the necessary steps so that, if possible, T.C.A. would choose the Caravelle.

I should like to direct a specific question to the Minister of Transport. I hope he will reply directly because otherwise we shall be obliged to spend two days on his estimates. I ask him if he shares the views expressed by Mr. McGregor as to the capacity of French Canadians to take their place in T.C.A.

I do not want to repeat what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has said with regard to Transair. There is, naturally, concern that they are abandoning this particular leg of this run on January 10. I understand they have the equipment, valued, according to some estimates, at $1 million or more. T.C.A. is reported to be losing $230,000 a year on serving this route. Transair has been serving the route for less than a year. Surely this company is not going to get out of the duty which it accepted to serve this run. I ask, what is the relationship between T.C.A.

and Transair Limited with regard to the ownership of this equipment, in view of the fact that they are getting out of the unprofitable portion of the run to serve the profitable portion of this run, and the service to the community is being denied.

Mr. Chairman, I see that some people feel frustrated. Those who are not allowed by their whip to take part in the debate would like to prevent from speaking those who are free to do so. We shall give them the opportunity of getting rid of their complexes and to say what is on their minds in this house. It will do them good, I believe.
Reference was made earlier to the article written by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). Personally, I thought it was better not to mention it, because I have known for a long time that when the hon. member refers to something else than Maurice Richard and Lili St. Cyr, he talks nonsense.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) termed the whole thing as gossip and I think it was rather improper of him to do so, because hardly two days ago, he made so bold as to rave and gossip-
Does the hon. member allow me a question?
Yes.
Has the hon. member paid his $3,000?

Mr. Chairman, I paid $1,671 in income tax to the federal government, and this is due to the bad administration under the Conservative government as well as under the Liberal government at the present time.
As for the rest, I say that the hon. member for Three Rivers has only gossiped just like his Conservative colleagues of the province of Quebec.
However, I wish to point out a fact. Several persons, among whom some newspapermen, have asked us whether pressures had been brought to bear on us or whether we had obtained some information from the French embassy about the Caravelle aircraft, or whether questions had been suggested that we should ask the president of T.C.A., and so on.
In view of the rumours abroad, I wanted to deny that we had ever been in touch, that any member of our group had ever been in touch with the French embassy, concerning the Caravelle or anything else for that matter, and that the embassy had brought pressure to bear on us.

Mr. Chairman, since there has been some mention in the last few minutes of the uneconomical flights operated by T.C.A. and in view of the fact that, this week, attention was drawn to the unfair competition on the part of this crown corporation which operates small uneconomical routes from one end of the country to the other, I should like to make a few remarks-

speechtext: Would the hon. member for Beauce permit me to interrupt him for a moment? It would appear to me that it is eleven o'clock and that we are unlikely to get this particular item through. Perhaps the committee, in the next thirty seconds, would consider dealing with the balance of the items in this department and we could hold over this particular item until tomorrow morning. I think that would create a better psychological situation. I do not intend to suggest that we should extend the time in order to do this.
I think the minister is aware that I have a long anticipated date with him on one of the other items.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman object to the other items passing, except this one and the other with which he wants to deal.
The suggestion is that we should stand this item. Is that the proposal?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It would appear to me now that the best thing to do is regard it as being eleven o'clock.
Carry on.

I should like to call it eleven o'clock and suggest to the committee that we meet tomorrow at ten rather than eleven and dispense with the question period. We could consider what would be done about the luncheon hour in the light of the progress being made and we would be in a better position to determine how long the session would go.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think that is a most constructive suggestion and I hope it will commend itself to all members of the committee. Perhaps when the Speaker is in the chair we could have an order made along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Timiska-ming, that we meet at ten o'clock, dispense with the question period, go right into committee of supply and get on with our business.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The only thing I think is wrong with that is the waiving of the question period. That is unsound. Something might happen in the interval. We do not object to sitting at ten o'clock.
Supply-Transport

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Last night the hon. gentleman was ready to prorogue tonight, in which case there would have been no question period on Saturday, so we would be giving up something which, if his expectations had been realized, would not have existed. I suggest we accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Timiskaming.
If we want to complete these estimates it is important that the Minister of Transport should answer the direct question I put to him.
Would the house consider a compromise and limit the question period to 30 minutes definite?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Fifteen.
Mr. Chairman, surely we should waive the question period entirely. It is a Saturday and not a normal sitting day. There is not going to be too much press coverage come out of it anyway on a Saturday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: There may not be very many answers come out of it either, but I think parliament exists as an institution which requires a question period. Thirty minutes as has been suggested is all right but let us not bargain everything away.
It is not a question of publicity.
Oh, oh.

We work for the public interest.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is the understanding of the Chair that we will meet toworrow at ten o'clock and that there will be a 30 minute limitation on the question period. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is so ordered.
What about the balance of the day? Do we rise from one to two?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I understand the other place has adjourned to meet at one o'clock. I would hope that if there was some reasonable prospect of concluding our business by say, two o'clock we would not rise for lunch, but if we were going to go on all day perhaps we could rise between one and two. If it could be understood that there would not be any objection taken to making a decision at that time and taking the general sense of the committee at that time, it seems to me that that would be the best arrangement.
